guides.title: Best Beaches in the Canary Islands: 20 Picks by Island
guides.summary: Twenty Canary Islands beaches on six islands, from Tenerife to La Palma, with honest notes on access, wind and currents and the official 2026 Blue Flag list.
guides.html:
The Canary Islands have two kinds of coast, and choosing a beach is mostly about knowing which one you are on. Sheltered south and east shores, often with breakwaters or reefs, give calm water for swimming. Exposed north and west coasts face the open Atlantic, with big surf, strong currents and beaches where a swim can be dangerous on an ordinary day. Sand colour varies too: golden and white on Fuerteventura, much of Gran Canaria and parts of Lanzarote; dark volcanic sand on much of Tenerife and La Palma.

Below are twenty beaches, first island by island and then sorted by what they suit. Each name links to its own page with fuller details. Blue Flag status comes from the official list for 2026 published by ADEAC, the Blue Flag operator in Spain, which awarded 52 beaches in 29 municipalities across the Canary Islands. A Blue Flag means water quality, safety and services met the standard for that season; it says nothing about how beautiful a beach is, and many fine wild beaches never apply.

Before you swim: flags, currents and lifeguards

Atlantic swell can arrive on a sunny, calm-looking day. On beaches with lifeguards, a green flag means swimming is allowed, yellow means take care and red means do not go in. On wild beaches there may be no flag and no one watching. Choose a beach with lifeguards, follow their instructions and stay out of the water when waves are breaking hard. The emergency number is 112 on every island; see emergency contacts.

Tenerife

Playa de las Teresitas is the beach for Santa Cruz, by the village of San Andrés in the north-east. The island tourism board lists it at 1,300 metres of pale sand, with breakwaters built to calm the waves, plus toilets, showers and bars. Check the flags and lifeguard advice before swimming.

Playa del Duque in Adeje is the smart end of Costa Adeje: 390 metres of sand with sun loungers, changing rooms and a large car park. El Duque (Sur) holds a Blue Flag for 2026.

Playa de El Médano, in Granadilla de Abona near Tenerife South Airport, is 750 metres of fine grey sand below the Montaña Roja volcanic cone. The tourism board notes that the far end from the town is the best place for windsurfing and kitesurfing. That says a lot: it is often windy, which suits sailors more than sunbathers.

Playa Jardín in Puerto de la Cruz is a dark-sand beach landscaped with gardens, a project by the Lanzarote artist César Manrique. It faces the north Atlantic, so the surf can be strong; watch the flags.

Playa de Benijo lies at the far north-east tip of the island, below the Anaga Rural Park. It is a wild black-sand beach reached down a path from the road, with sea stacks offshore and big Atlantic waves. Go for the scenery and the sunset; do not use a calm-looking sea as a reason to swim.

Gran Canaria

Playa de las Canteras is the city beach of Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, a long strip of golden sand with a walkway full of cafés. Its natural reef, La Barra, protects a large part of the beach from the open sea, giving calm water for swimming and snorkelling. The southern end, near the Alfredo Kraus Auditorium, is where surfers gather.

Playa de Maspalomas runs along the edge of the Maspalomas dunes nature reserve to the 56-metre lighthouse, in the resort area of Maspalomas. Long stretches have no buildings, and parts are traditionally used by naturists. Blue Flag for 2026.

Playa del Inglés joins Maspalomas to the north-east and is the busy, fully serviced end of the same sweep of sand, with sunbeds and beach bars. Check local surf conditions before entering the water. Blue Flag for 2026 (listed as El Inglés).

Playa de Amadores, in the south-west near Puerto de Mogán, is a man-made beach of light sand behind protective breakwaters. The island tourism board describes its sea as gentle, but check the flags and supervise children closely.

Playa de Güigüí is the opposite: a remote beach on the west coast with no road. You reach it by a long, steep hike over the ridge from the Tasartico area, or by boat. Do not rely on finding services or lifeguards; check the sea conditions and prepare for a strenuous return walk. Take plenty of water and start early.

Lanzarote and La Graciosa

Playas de Papagayo are a string of coves east of Playa Blanca in the south of Lanzarote. The island tourism board lists fine white sand and calm water, with parking but no public transport. Access is by an unpaved track, and services are limited, so bring what you need.

Playa de Famara is a long, open beach on the north-west coast below the Famara cliffs. The tourism board lists strong waves and wind, hazard signs and lifeguards, and it is Lanzarote's surfing beach. Strong surf makes this a poor choice for casual swimming; follow the lifeguards and hazard signs.

Playa Grande is the main beach of Puerto del Carmen: about 1,190 metres of golden sand with calm water, lifeguards, sunbeds, showers and a promenade. It regained its Blue Flag for 2026 (listed as Grande (Blanca), Tías).

Caletón Blanco, near Órzola in the north of the island (municipality of Haría), is a set of white-sand coves among black lava. The tourism board lists calm water and suitability for families; check the tide and conditions around the rocks. It is a good stop before or after the boat to La Graciosa.

Playa de las Conchas on La Graciosa is a wide, empty beach facing the islet of Montaña Clara. Getting there means a boat from Órzola and then a walk, bike ride or 4x4 taxi across the island, using the island’s unpaved tracks. The currents here are strong and swimming can be dangerous; many visitors come for the view and the walk rather than the water. Our island-hopping guide covers the ferry.

Fuerteventura

Grandes Playas de Corralejo run south of Corralejo along the edge of the Corralejo dunes natural park, with the main road behind the dunes and the island of Lobos offshore. Wind is common and some stretches catch waves, so check conditions before swimming. Grandes Playas holds a Blue Flag for 2026.

Playa de Sotavento on the Jandía peninsula in the south is a very long beach where a lagoon forms behind a sandbar at low tide. It is known for windsurfing and kitesurfing: the steady trade wind that makes it ideal for sailors can make an afternoon on the sand gritty.

Playa de Cofete lies on the remote north-west side of Jandía, reached by an unpaved mountain track from the Morro Jable side. It is spectacular, with the Jandía massif behind a huge empty beach, but the Atlantic here can be hazardous and you should not rely on lifeguard cover. Do not swim. Check your hire car terms before driving the track.

Playa de La Concha and the El Cotillo lagoons are on the north-west coast near the village of El Cotillo. A rocky reef shelters La Concha and the lagoons beside it, so the water inside is calmer than the open coast nearby; it is a favourite with families. La Concha holds a Blue Flag for 2026.

La Palma

Playa de Tazacorte, at Puerto de Tazacorte on the west coast of La Palma, is a black-sand beach beside the harbour, with restaurants nearby. It holds a Blue Flag for 2026 (listed as El Puerto de Tazacorte). Combine it with the Caldera de Taburiente National Park or the Roque de los Muchachos.

The same beaches, sorted by what they suit

Families and calm water

Playa de las Teresitas, Playa del Duque, Playa de las Canteras (inside the reef), Playa de Amadores, Playa Grande in Puerto del Carmen, Caletón Blanco, La Concha at El Cotillo and Playa de Tazacorte. Check the individual beach page for nearby services.

Long natural beaches

Playa de Maspalomas, Playa del Inglés, the Grandes Playas de Corralejo and Playa de Sotavento: long walks, dunes or lagoons, and room for a beach walk.

Wind and waves

El Médano and Sotavento for windsurfing and kitesurfing; Famara and the surf end of Las Canteras for surfing. Corralejo's beaches also catch wind and swell.

Wild beaches reached on foot or by track

Benijo, Güigüí, Papagayo, Playa de las Conchas and Cofete. Bring water, shade and food, check access and lifeguard cover, and treat the sea at Güigüí, Las Conchas and Cofete with real caution.

Blue Flags in this guide (2026)

From the twenty beaches above, the official 2026 ADEAC list includes: Playa del Duque (El Duque Sur, Adeje), Playa de Maspalomas and Playa del Inglés (San Bartolomé de Tirajana), Playa Grande (Tías, Lanzarote), Grandes Playas and La Concha (La Oliva, Fuerteventura) and El Puerto de Tazacorte (La Palma). Las Canteras, Las Teresitas, El Médano, Amadores, Papagayo and the wild beaches are not on the 2026 list.

When to go and planning

The islands have beach weather all year, but the sea is coolest in late winter and the trade wind is usually strongest in summer. See best time to visit and the weather page. For snorkelling and diving spots, see snorkelling. To choose an island first, read which Canary Island is best, and browse every listing on the beaches hub.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which Canary Island has the best beaches?

For long golden or white sand, Fuerteventura and the south of Gran Canaria are hard to beat. Lanzarote has the sheltered coves of Papagayo and the town beach of Puerto del Carmen. Tenerife offers pale sand at Las Teresitas and Playa del Duque, and black sand at Playa Jardín and Benijo.

Which Canary Islands beaches are best for children?

Calm, serviced beaches: Playa de Amadores and Las Canteras (inside the reef) on Gran Canaria, Las Teresitas and Playa del Duque on Tenerife, Playa Grande on Lanzarote and La Concha at El Cotillo on Fuerteventura. Avoid Cofete, Famara, Benijo and Las Conchas with small children in the water.

Which Canary Islands beaches have a Blue Flag in 2026?

ADEAC awarded 52 beaches in the Canary Islands for 2026. Among the beaches in this guide, Playa del Duque, Maspalomas, Playa del Inglés, Playa Grande in Puerto del Carmen, Grandes Playas de Corralejo, La Concha at El Cotillo and Puerto de Tazacorte are on the list.

Is it safe to swim at Cofete?

No. Cofete is an exposed Atlantic beach with hazardous sea conditions. Do not rely on lifeguard cover. Enjoy the walk and the view, and swim at a sheltered beach instead.

Are there black sand beaches in the Canary Islands?

Yes, many, especially on Tenerife and La Palma. Playa Jardín in Puerto de la Cruz, Benijo in Anaga and Playa de Tazacorte on La Palma are good examples. Dark sand gets very hot in the afternoon sun, so bring beach shoes.

Can you reach Playa de Güigüí by car?

No. Güigüí on Gran Canaria's west coast has no road. You walk in over a steep ridge or arrive by boat, so plan for a long, hot hike with no services at the beach.

Where is the best beach for kitesurfing in the Canary Islands?

Playa de Sotavento on Fuerteventura and El Médano on Tenerife are established options; conditions vary with the wind. Learn with a licensed school and follow the zones marked for kites and swimmers.

guides.title: Best Time to Visit the Canary Islands: Month by Month
guides.summary: The Canary Islands work all year. October to April is the winter-sun season; May, June, September and October suit a mixed trip. Compare stations by coast.
guides.html:
The short answer

There is no bad month to visit the Canary Islands. Average daytime highs at the main coastal airports stay between roughly 20C and 29C across the year, rain is scarce on the coasts, and winter swimming comfort depends on your tolerance for cool water. The real question is what you want from the trip.

  • Winter sun (November to March): a season to consider for a break from the UK or Irish winter. At Tenerife Sur airport, November to March average highs range from 21.7 to 24.8C, short days and the year's few rainy spells. See our Canary Islands in winter guide for detail.
  • All-round comfort (May, June, September and October): warm, dry, long days, and a sea that is warmest in September and October.
  • Peak summer (July and August): the hottest and sunniest months, busy with Spanish and European family holidays.
  • Walking: spring and autumn suit the trails of Teide National Park, Garajonay on La Gomera and Caldera de Taburiente on La Palma best.

Where the figures in this guide come from

All air temperatures, rainfall and sunshine figures below are the standard climate values (normales climatológicos) published by AEMET, the Spanish state weather agency, for named stations. AEMET's station pages give these values for the reference period 1981 to 2010, so we use that one period everywhere to keep the islands comparable. They are long-run averages, not a forecast; for the current outlook see our weather page.

The stations are Tenerife Sur airport (64 m above sea level, in Granadilla de Abona), Santa Cruz de Tenerife (36 m, the capital), Tenerife Norte airport (632 m, in San Cristóbal de La Laguna), Gran Canaria airport (24 m, on the east coast in Ingenio), Lanzarote airport (14 m), Fuerteventura airport (25 m) and La Palma airport (33 m, on the east coast). For altitude we use Izaña, an AEMET observatory at 2,369 m in the highlands of Tenerife.

North, south and altitude

The single most useful thing to know about Canary weather is that the larger, higher islands have two climates. The northeast trade winds push moist air against the northern slopes of Tenerife, Gran Canaria and La Palma, where it builds a band of cloud on the hillsides. The southern and southwestern coasts sit in the lee of the mountains and stay drier and sunnier.

The AEMET figures show it clearly on Tenerife. Tenerife Sur airport, near the resorts of Costa Adeje, Playa de las Américas and Los Cristianos, averages 132 mm of rain a year over about 15 rainy days and logs 193 hours of sunshine in January. Tenerife Norte airport, up on the plateau near La Laguna, averages 520 mm over about 64 rainy days and 150 hours of January sun, and its winter highs are five or six degrees lower. Part of that gap is altitude (632 m): Santa Cruz, at sea level, is much closer to the south in temperature. Puerto de la Cruz, at sea level on the north coast, is greener and cloudier than the south but warmer than the airport on the plateau above it.

Altitude matters as much as aspect. At Izaña, 2,369 m up, January averages a high of 7.5C and a low of 1.1C, AEMET records an average of about two snow days a month from December to March, and July averages a high of 23.0C. If you plan to ride the Teide cable car, whose upper station is at 3,555 m, or follow our Teide permit and cable car guide, pack a warm layer in any month. The same applies to Roque Nublo in the centre of Gran Canaria and the Roque de los Muchachos on La Palma.

Lanzarote and Fuerteventura are lower and flatter, so they lack the cloud belt and stay dry: Lanzarote airport averages 111 mm of rain a year and Fuerteventura airport 98 mm. They also feel the trade wind more, which is why Corralejo and Playa de Sotavento are known for windsurfing and kitesurfing.

Summer is close to rainless: from June to August the coastal stations average 2 mm of rain a month or less, and even Tenerife Norte averages only 5 to 11 mm.

Sea temperature

The Atlantic around the islands is cooler than the latitude suggests. For a consistent long-run figure we use NOAA's OI SST V2 monthly climatology for 1991 to 2020 at the offshore grid point 27.5N 16W, south of the channel between Tenerife and Gran Canaria, matching our weather page. On that basis the sea averages about 20C in January and 19C from February to April, 20C in May, 21 to 22C in June and July, 23C in August, and peaks at about 23C in September and October before easing to 22C in November and 21C in December.

The warmest swimming therefore comes after the warmest air: September and October suit long swims and snorkelling best. It is an open-ocean average for one grid cell, so the water at a given beach on a given day can differ. Look for lifeguarded, reef-sheltered beaches such as Las Canteras in Las Palmas and follow the flags before swimming.

Month by month

January and February

The heart of winter sun. Highs average 21 to 22C in the south of Tenerife and around 21C at the Gran Canaria, Lanzarote and Fuerteventura airports, with lows near 14 to 15C. The north of Tenerife and La Palma see more cloud than the south. Snow is most likely on the Teide heights now. The Three Kings parades on 5 January close the Christmas season, and Carnival begins to dominate from late January.

March and April

Days lengthen and highs edge up to about 22 to 23.5C at the coastal airports, while the sea is at its coolest, about 19C. March still has a few rainy days, April far fewer. This is good walking weather in Anaga, Masca and the western islands. Easter falls on 28 March in 2027, with Maundy Thursday and Good Friday as public holidays (see our 2027 public holidays guide).

May and June

Often overlooked and among the most comfortable months. Highs reach 24 to 26C, rain all but stops, and sunshine hours climb: Lanzarote airport averages 297 hours in May. Trade-wind cloud can sit over the north coasts in early summer. Canary Islands Day on 30 May brings folk music and traditional dress, and the flower and sand carpets of Corpus Christi in La Orotava follow in late May or June, depending on the date of Easter.

July and August

The hottest months, with highs of about 27 to 29C at sea level and July sunshine of around 300 hours at the southern and eastern airports. Spanish and European family holidays peak now. Brief hotter spells can arrive with winds off Africa (see calima, below). High ground is pleasant in the day but still cool at night. Early August brings the Bajada de la Rama in Agaete on Gran Canaria.

September and October

Our pick for an all-round trip: highs still 26 to 29C, the warmest sea of the year at about 23C, and calmer resorts once the school holidays end. Rain starts to return to the north towards the end of October. Good months for diving and for whale and dolphin watching off southwest Tenerife.

November and December

The winter-sun season restarts. November highs average about 24C on the coasts and December about 22C, and December is the wettest month at every station in the table above, though on the southern coasts that still means only a few rainy days. Compare availability before choosing Christmas or New Year dates.

Calima: Saharan dust

Calima is the haze of fine dust that arrives when easterly or southeasterly winds carry air from the Sahara over the islands. During an episode the sky turns milky or orange, visibility drops, and air quality worsens; AEMET described an intense February 2021 episode that left the islands almost hidden under atmospheric dust. Episodes usually last a few days and are not limited to summer: the 2021 episode came in February. People with asthma or heart and lung conditions should follow local health advice and AEMET warnings while one lasts.

Crowds and prices

Compare flight and room prices for your dates, including nearby weeks if your plans are flexible. Check school holidays and the Carnival programme before choosing a city base; do not assume a particular month will be cheaper or quieter.

Carnival season

Carnival is a major event of the Canary year, with celebrations including the Santa Cruz de Tenerife Carnival and the Las Palmas de Gran Canaria Carnival, with smaller carnivals across the islands and Los Indianos in Santa Cruz de La Palma on Carnival Monday. Dates move each year with Easter and with each city council's programme. For 2027, Las Palmas de Gran Canaria has Carnival Tuesday on 9 February as a local holiday, while Santa Cruz de Tenerife has moved its celebrations later than usual: its local holiday for Carnival Tuesday is 23 February 2027, and the council has said the street carnival will run from 19 to 28 February. Check the official programme before booking, and book rooms early for those weeks.

Which month for what

  • Warmest sea: September and October.
  • Driest weather: June to August at the named stations.
  • Winter warmth: the south of Tenerife and Gran Canaria, around Maspalomas, and the low eastern islands such as Lanzarote and Fuerteventura.
  • Hiking: March to June and October to November; see hiking in the Canary Islands.
  • Choosing an island first? Read which Canary Island is best.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the best month to visit the Canary Islands?

For a balance of warm air, warm sea, dry weather and fewer crowds, September and October are hard to beat: highs of about 26 to 29C at the coastal airports and the sea at its warmest, about 23C. For winter sun, January to March offers highs of about 21 to 23C on the southern coasts.

Which Canary Island is warmest in winter?

The differences between the coastal airports are small: January highs average 21.7C at Tenerife Sur, 20.8C at Gran Canaria airport, 20.7C at Lanzarote airport and 20.6C at Fuerteventura airport (AEMET, 1981 to 2010). Where you stay on the island matters more: the south of Tenerife and Gran Canaria is sunnier and drier than the north.

When does it rain in the Canary Islands?

Most rain falls from October to March, with December the wettest month at the main stations. Summer is almost completely dry. The north of Tenerife and La Palma get far more rain than the south of Tenerife or the eastern islands.

Is the sea warm enough to swim in winter?

The long-run average sea temperature between Tenerife and Gran Canaria is about 20C in January and 19C from February to April and about 23C in September and October (NOAA OI SST V2, 1991 to 2020).

Is it cold on Mount Teide?

Yes, compared with the coast. AEMET's Izaña observatory, at 2,369 m, averages a January high of 7.5C and a low of 1.1C, with snow on about two days a month from December to March. The cable car's upper station is higher still, at 3,555 m.

When is Carnival in the Canary Islands in 2027?

Each city sets its own dates. In 2027 Las Palmas de Gran Canaria has its Carnival Tuesday holiday on 9 February, and Santa Cruz de Tenerife on 23 February, with street events announced for 19 to 28 February. Check the official programmes nearer the time.

guides.title: Canary Islands in Winter: December to February Guide
guides.summary: From December to February the Canary Islands coastal airports average highs of about 21 to 23C and lows of about 14 to 17C, and the sea sits near 19 to 21C.
guides.html:
Is the Canary Islands winter really warm?

Warm by northern European standards, yes; hot, no. Between December and February the coastal airports on the main islands average daytime highs of about 21 to 23C and night-time lows of about 14 to 17C, according to the standard climate values that AEMET, the Spanish state weather agency, publishes for each station (reference period 1981 to 2010). These station averages help visitors from the UK and Ireland plan a winter break. It also means evenings that call for a jumper, a sea that is refreshing rather than balmy, and the occasional grey or wet day.

The rest of this guide covers which island and which coast to choose, the sea, daylight, the mountains, the festive calendar and what to pack. For the whole year, see our best time to visit the Canary Islands guide.

Which coasts are warmest and driest

The table shows that the island you choose matters less than where on it you stay. All the sea-level airports sit within about a degree of one another for daytime highs. The big differences are cloud and rain, and they follow the mountains.

  • South and southwest Tenerife. Tenerife Sur airport averages 1.8 days of rain in January and 193 hours of sunshine, among the highest January figures of the coastal stations in the table. This is the coast of Costa Adeje, Playa de las Américas and Los Cristianos, served by Tenerife South airport.
  • South Gran Canaria. Maspalomas, Playa del Inglés and Meloneras and Puerto de Mogán sit in the lee of the island's central peaks. AEMET's nearest station in this guide is Gran Canaria airport on the east coast, so treat its figures as a guide rather than an exact match for the resorts.
  • Lanzarote and Fuerteventura. The two driest coastal airport references in this table, with 63 mm and 56 mm over the three months at their airports, and Lanzarote airport records 203 hours of January sun. Nights are a little cooler (about 14C in January) and the trade wind is a frequent companion, which suits surfers and kitesurfers more than sunbathers on exposed beaches. Sheltered options include the Papagayo beaches near Playa Blanca and the lagoons at El Cotillo.
  • North Tenerife and La Palma. Greener and noticeably wetter. Tenerife Norte airport, at 632 m near La Laguna, gets 232 mm across the winter months and averages only 16 to 17C by day; The Santa Cruz station is much milder than the upland airport. Puerto de la Cruz has a separate coastal setting; do not transfer the airport averages directly to its beaches. La Palma airport averages 186 mm over the three months. These are rewarding winter destinations for walkers and for culture, just not the surest choice for a week on a sun lounger.

Sea temperature in winter

Using NOAA's OI SST V2 monthly climatology for 1991 to 2020 at the offshore grid point 27.5N 16W, south of the channel between Tenerife and Gran Canaria, matching our weather page, the sea averages about 21C in December, 20C in January and 19C in February, its coolest month alongside March. Plenty of visitors swim; many others find it bracing. Check whether your hotel pool is heated, or consider Siam Park on Tenerife as an alternative to the sea. For the most sheltered sea swimming, look at beaches that face away from the swell, such as reef-sheltered Las Canteras in Las Palmas or Playa del Duque on the southwest coast of Tenerife, and always follow the beach flag.

Daylight

The islands lie far south of the UK, so winter days are noticeably longer. Using the US Naval Observatory's sun calculator for Santa Cruz de Tenerife, sunrise on 21 December 2026 is at about 07:53 and sunset at about 18:13 local time, a little over 10 hours 20 minutes of daylight. By 28 February 2027, sunrise is at about 07:31 and sunset at about 19:04, roughly 11 and a half hours. The Canary Islands keep Western European Time, one hour behind mainland Spain and the same as the UK and Ireland in winter, so the sun rises later in the morning than many visitors expect.

Snow on Teide

Winter is the season for snow on the high ground of Tenerife. AEMET's Izaña observatory, at 2,369 m in Tenerife’s highlands, averages a January high of 7.5C and a low of 1.1C, with about 1.6 snow days in December, 2.4 in January and 2.5 in February. The summit itself, and the upper station of the Teide cable car at 3,555 m, are colder still. After a snowfall, check road status and the cable car operator's notices before driving up. Wear proper layers, gloves and a hat in Teide National Park, and read our Teide permit and cable car guide if you plan to reach the summit. Clear, cold winter nights are also excellent for stargazing.

Christmas, New Year and Three Kings

Christmas Day (25 December) and New Year's Day are public holidays, and expect quieter streets and more closures on those days in towns away from the resorts. In Spain the main day for children's presents is traditionally 6 January, Epiphany, which is also a public holiday in the Canary Islands. The evening before, 5 January, towns across the islands hold Three Kings parades, when the kings arrive and throw sweets to children. Compare flights and hotel availability early if you plan to travel at Christmas or New Year. Our Canary Islands public holidays 2027 guide lists every date for the coming year, including Tenerife's island holiday on Tuesday 2 February 2027 for the Virgen de la Candelaria.

Carnival

Late January and February belong to Carnival, a major festival across the islands. Two celebrations to consider are the Santa Cruz de Tenerife Carnival and the Las Palmas de Gran Canaria Carnival, with Los Indianos, the white-clothes and talcum-powder party in Santa Cruz de La Palma, on Carnival Monday (see Los Indianos). In 2027 the dates diverge. Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, La Laguna and several other municipalities have Carnival Tuesday on 9 February as a local holiday. Santa Cruz de Tenerife has moved its carnival later than usual: its Carnival Tuesday local holiday is 23 February 2027, and the city council has announced street celebrations from 19 to 28 February. Santa Cruz has published its official programme; check each city’s current programme before booking.

What to pack

  • Summer clothes for the day on the southern coasts, plus a warm layer or light jacket for evenings, which drop to about 14 to 17C.
  • A waterproof if you will spend time in the north of Tenerife, on La Palma or walking in Anaga or Garajonay.
  • Proper winter clothing (hat, gloves, fleece and shell) for Teide, Roque Nublo or any trip above about 2,000 m.
  • High-factor sun cream: the winter sun is still strong at this latitude.
  • Walking shoes with grip for volcanic trails; see hiking.

What not to expect

  • Guaranteed unbroken sun. Winter is when most of the year's rain falls, and a cloudy or wet spell of a day or two can happen anywhere, especially in the north.
  • Warm evenings. Dinner outdoors is pleasant in the south, but you will want sleeves.
  • A warm sea. About 19 to 21C is swimmable but cool.
  • Calm water everywhere. Winter Atlantic swells can make north-facing beaches rough; that is why surfers come.
  • Clear skies every day. Episodes of calima, the haze of Saharan dust, can occur in winter: AEMET reported an intense one in February 2021.
  • Empty resorts. Compare availability around Christmas, February half-term and the Carnival weekends before choosing your dates.

Choosing your winter base

For the surest sun, stay in the south of Tenerife or Gran Canaria, or on Lanzarote or Fuerteventura and pick a sheltered beach. For walking, try La Gomera or La Palma. For city life, Carnival and a beach in town, choose Las Palmas de Gran Canaria. Still undecided? Compare all eight in which Canary Island is best.

Frequently Asked Questions

How warm are the Canary Islands in December, January and February?

At the coastal airports, AEMET's 1981 to 2010 averages give highs of about 22 to 23C in December and 21 to 22C in January and February, with lows of about 14 to 17C. Higher ground is much cooler: Tenerife Norte airport, at 632 m, averages a January high of 16.0C.

Which Canary Island is warmest in winter?

The sea-level airports on Tenerife, Gran Canaria, Lanzarote and Fuerteventura are within about a degree of each other. Tenerife Sur airport has the highest January average high of those stations, 21.7C. For sun and dry weather, the south of Tenerife and Gran Canaria and the eastern islands are the best bets.

Can you swim in the sea in winter?

Yes, if you do not mind cool water. The long-run sea temperature between Tenerife and Gran Canaria averages about 21C in December and 20C in January and 19C in February (NOAA OI SST V2, 1991 to 2020). Choose sheltered beaches and follow lifeguard flags.

Does it snow in the Canary Islands?

Snow can fall on high ground. AEMET's Izaña observatory on Tenerife, at 2,369 m, averages about two snow days a month from December to February. Use the mountain forecast for high-altitude trips.

How many hours of daylight are there in winter?

About 10 hours 20 minutes at the winter solstice in Santa Cruz de Tenerife, rising to about 11 and a half hours by the end of February, according to US Naval Observatory sun data.

Is January or February better?

The averages are almost identical. February is fractionally warmer by day at most stations. Check the Carnival programme and compare availability after Three Kings on 5 and 6 January.

Is the Canary Islands busy in winter?

Demand depends on your island, dates and local events. Compare availability around Christmas, New Year, school holidays and the published Carnival programmes.

guides.title: Canary Islands Island Hopping: Ferries, Flights, Day Trips
guides.summary: Ferry routes and crossing times between the Canary Islands from the operators' own pages, the best day-trip pairs, hire cars on board and fare discounts.
guides.html:
Every inhabited Canary Island is linked by sea, and several crossings are short enough for a day trip. From Playa Blanca in Lanzarote the ferry reaches Corralejo in Fuerteventura in about half an hour; from Los Cristianos in Tenerife it is under an hour to La Gomera; and a small boat from Órzola in the north of Lanzarote takes about 25 minutes to La Graciosa. Longer hops, such as Gran Canaria to La Palma, take several hours by sea, which is where the inter-island planes earn their keep.

Crossing times and fares below come from the operators' own pages as read in November 2026; timetables change by season, so check the operator before you build a day around a sailing.

The ferry operators

Fred. Olsen Express runs fast ferries and trimarans across the archipelago. Its route list, as of November 2026, covers Lanzarote and Fuerteventura (Playa Blanca and Corralejo), Tenerife and La Gomera (Los Cristianos and San Sebastián de La Gomera), Tenerife and Gran Canaria (Santa Cruz de Tenerife and Agaete), Tenerife to La Palma and to El Hierro, Gran Canaria to Fuerteventura (Las Palmas and Morro Jable), and longer links from Gran Canaria to La Gomera, La Palma and El Hierro. It also runs a coastal service on La Gomera between San Sebastián, Playa de Santiago and Valle Gran Rey.

Baleària Canarias sells the sailings long associated with Naviera Armas: the old navieraarmas.com address now redirects to the Armas Trasmediterránea site, whose Canary routes and timetables sit on baleariacanarias.com. Its route pages list Los Cristianos to San Sebastián de La Gomera, Playa Blanca to Corralejo, Las Palmas de Gran Canaria to Santa Cruz de Tenerife, and connections between Tenerife, Gran Canaria, La Palma, El Hierro, Lanzarote and Fuerteventura.

La Graciosa has its own small passenger ferries from Órzola, run by local companies including Biosfera Express and Líneas Romero. Visitors cannot take cars on these passenger ferries. Authorised vehicles, including local taxis, operate on La Graciosa.

Main routes and crossing times

These are the crossing times each operator publishes for its own sailings, as of November 2026. Departures per day are maximums and vary by season and day of the week.

Fred. Olsen also runs a free Ferry Bus for its passengers on two routes: from Parque Santa Catalina in Las Palmas to the port of Agaete for the Tenerife sailing, and from the Santa Cruz de Tenerife bus station to Los Cristianos for sailings to La Gomera, La Palma and El Hierro. Seats are limited and the company asks you to book them at least 48 hours ahead. For buses on each island, see our transportation guide.

Inter-island flights

Binter Canarias operates inter-island flights. Flights make most sense for long hops where the sea route takes three hours or more, such as Lanzarote or Fuerteventura to La Palma, or Gran Canaria to El Hierro. On the islands with airport pages you will land at Tenerife North (TFN), an inter-island departure airport, Gran Canaria (LPA), Lanzarote (ACE), Fuerteventura (FUE) or La Palma (SPC). The small airports on La Gomera (GMZ) and El Hierro (VDE) are inter-island fields: Aena, the airport operator, lists daily Binter routes from La Gomera to Gran Canaria and to Tenerife North. Canaryfly also sells inter-island flights.

Before choosing a plane over a boat, add the time it takes to reach the airport, check in and get into town at the other end. For Tenerife to La Gomera, or Lanzarote to Fuerteventura, compare the ferry with the whole flight journey. If you arrive from abroad at Tenerife South (TFS), remember that Tenerife North is a different airport: check the airport code on each flight and allow for the transfer.

Three easy day trips

Lanzarote to Fuerteventura: Playa Blanca and Corralejo

A short crossing between Lanzarote and Fuerteventura. Both operators sail it, and the frequency makes a relaxed day possible: walk off the boat in Corralejo, spend the day on the Grandes Playas de Corralejo inside the Corralejo dunes natural park, and sail back in the evening. With a car you can push on to the lagoons at El Cotillo on the north-west coast. The trip works just as well from the Fuerteventura side to see Papagayo or the vineyards of La Geria.

Tenerife to La Gomera: Los Cristianos and San Sebastián

Los Cristianos is in Arona, on Tenerife's south coast. If you are staying in Costa Adeje, plan your transfer to Los Cristianos port before booking the ferry. The 50-minute crossing lands you in San Sebastián, the island capital. La Gomera is steep and its roads are slow, so a day trip is best spent either in San Sebastián itself or on a route up to the laurel forest of Garajonay National Park and the Mirador de Abrante above Agulo. Without a car, an organised excursion is the simpler choice.

Lanzarote to La Graciosa: Órzola

Órzola is a fishing village at the northern tip of Lanzarote, a short drive from the Mirador del Río, which looks straight down on La Graciosa. Boats land at Caleta de Sebo, the island's main village. There are no paved roads, so people walk, hire bikes or take one of the island's 4x4 taxis to beaches such as Playa de las Conchas. Biosfera Express listed a non-resident return fare of 29 euros for adults and 15 euros for children as of November 2026. Before you head for the port, the white-sand coves of Caletón Blanco are just outside Órzola.

Longer hops and multi-island trips

For two or three islands in one holiday, the common patterns are Lanzarote plus Fuerteventura, Tenerife plus La Gomera, and Gran Canaria plus Tenerife by the Agaete or Las Palmas ferries. The western islands of La Palma and El Hierro are best reached from Tenerife, either by the longer ferries or by plane. Our two-week island-hopping itinerary strings these together, and which Canary Island is best helps you choose where to base yourself. The island-hopping activity page gives a quick overview.

Taking a hire car on the ferry

Both main operators carry cars on most routes, but not on every boat. On Lanzarote to Fuerteventura, Fred. Olsen says its fast ferry Bocayna Express takes vehicles while the Buganvilla Express carries foot passengers only, so pick the right sailing when booking. Baleària Canarias says the Volcán de Tindaya on the same route carries passengers and vehicles.

Fred. Olsen sets out how to book with a hire car whose details you do not yet have: choose rental ('Rental' or 'RENT' under the make) and enter 0000XXX as the registration, then send the real details to the company or update them at a sales office no later than one hour before departure. Vehicles must be at the dock and ready to board 40 minutes before the departure time.

The hire company has the final say. We could not find a clause about inter-island ferries on the conditions page of the hire firm we checked, so ask your rental company in writing whether the car may leave the island, whether insurance still applies on board and on the other island, and whether a fee is charged. Visitors cannot take hire cars to La Graciosa on the passenger ferry.

Rough seas and disruption

The Canary Islands sit in the open Atlantic, and the trade winds and winter swells can make crossings rough. Fast ferries are more affected than you might expect: sailings can run late, be swapped to a different vessel or be cancelled in bad weather, and Biosfera Express notes that its crossing time depends mainly on the weather. Check the La Graciosa operator's service notices before travelling.

Do not plan a ferry on the same day as a flight home, especially from a smaller island. Check what your fare allows: Fred. Olsen states that on inter-island trips only its Flexible and Oro fares can be fully refunded, though tickets can be changed within a year. The weather page and Canary Islands in winter guide explain the seasonal pattern.

The resident discount does not apply to visitors

Fares advertised from a few euros are usually resident fares. Fred. Olsen describes a 75% discount for Canary Islands residents on inter-island trips, under Spanish rules (Royal Decree 1316/2001 and Decree 222/2000) that require proof of residence. Holidaymakers, and Spaniards who live elsewhere, pay the full fare. When you book online, leave the resident box unticked: a fare booked as a resident without the documents can be refused at boarding. The same applies to inter-island flights.

Fares change by date, fare type and vehicle, so we do not quote them here except where read on the operator's page (see the La Graciosa fare above). Compare both operators on routes they share.

Practical tips

  • Book ahead in peak weeks. Christmas, Easter and Spanish public holidays (see Canary Islands public holidays 2027) fill car decks early.
  • Carry ID. Ferries and inter-island flights are domestic Spanish journeys, but you still need a passport or national identity card to travel. See visa requirements for entry rules.
  • Know the port. Tenerife's main inter-island ferry ports are (Los Cristianos in the south and Santa Cruz in the north-east) and Gran Canaria's are Las Palmas and Agaete; check which one your ticket uses.
  • Emergencies. The number on every island is 112. See emergency contacts.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can you island hop in the Canary Islands by ferry?

Yes. Fred. Olsen Express and Baleària Canarias connect all the main islands, and local boats from Órzola serve La Graciosa. Short hops such as Playa Blanca to Corralejo (25 to 35 minutes) and Los Cristianos to La Gomera (about 50 minutes) are easy; longer hops to La Palma or El Hierro take two to four hours by sea.

How long is the ferry from Lanzarote to Fuerteventura?

Fred. Olsen Express gives 25 minutes on its fast ferry or 35 minutes on its other boat between Playa Blanca and Corralejo, with up to 12 departures a day. Baleària Canarias gives about 35 minutes, with up to seven sailings on weekdays and six at weekends, as of November 2026.

How do you get from Tenerife to La Gomera?

Take the ferry from Los Cristianos in south Tenerife to San Sebastián de La Gomera. Both Fred. Olsen Express and Baleària Canarias publish a crossing time of about 50 minutes. Fred. Olsen's free Ferry Bus links the Santa Cruz de Tenerife bus station with Los Cristianos if you are staying in the north. Binter also flies from Tenerife North to La Gomera's small airport.

Can I take a hire car on a Canary Islands ferry?

The ferry companies accept hire cars and explain how to book one, but your rental company decides whether its car may leave the island and whether insurance still applies. Ask in writing before you book. Visitors cannot bring cars on the passenger ferries to La Graciosa.

Is it cheaper to fly or take the ferry between the Canary Islands?

It depends on the route and date. For short crossings the ferry is usually simpler and avoids airport transfers. For longer hops, compare flight connections and total travel time. Compare both on the operators' own sites for your dates.

Do tourists get the Canary Islands resident discount?

No. The resident discount is for eligible Canary Islands residents who can meet the operator's documentation requirements. Visitors pay the full fare, and booking a resident fare without the documents can mean being refused at boarding.

Are ferries cancelled because of bad weather?

It happens, mainly in winter swells and strong trade winds, and either delays or cancellations can affect your plans. Check the La Graciosa operator's service notices before travelling. Keep a spare day before an international flight and check your fare's refund rules.

Can you visit La Graciosa as a day trip from Lanzarote?

Yes. Boats leave Órzola several times a day and take about 25 minutes. Once there you walk, cycle or take a 4x4 taxi, as the island has no paved roads and visitors cannot bring cars.

guides.title: Canary Islands Public Holidays 2027: Full Calendar
guides.summary: The Canary Islands have 11 archipelago-wide public holidays in 2027, plus one island holiday on each island and two local holidays in each municipality.
guides.html:
The 2027 calendar is official

The Canary Islands government fixed its 2027 public holidays in Decree 115/2026 of 29 June, published in the Boletín Oficial de Canarias (BOC), the regional gazette, on 3 July 2026. Spain's national Boletín Oficial del Estado (BOE) then listed the holidays of every region in a resolution of 8 October 2026, published on 13 October 2026. The local holidays of all 88 municipalities followed in an order of 7 August 2026, published in the BOC on 21 August 2026. Everything below comes from those three texts, and every weekday has been checked against the 2027 calendar.

Spain allows up to 14 paid public holidays a year: up to 12 set nationally and regionally, plus two local ones per municipality. In the Canary Islands that means three layers: holidays for the whole archipelago, one holiday for each island, and two for each town.

Holidays across all the Canary Islands in 2027

Canary Islands Day in 2027

Canary Islands Day (Día de Canarias) on 30 May is the archipelago's own regional day and in most years its own public holiday. In 2027, 30 May is a Sunday. The 2027 decree does not include it in the list of working holidays and does not move the day off to Monday 31 May, so Monday is a normal working day. Celebrations are still held around the date.

Easter 2027: Maundy Thursday and Good Friday

Easter Sunday falls on 28 March 2027. Both Maundy Thursday (25 March) and Good Friday (26 March) are public holidays in the Canary Islands, according to the regional decree and the BOE list. Easter Monday (29 March) is not a holiday in the Canary Islands; it is a holiday only in some other Spanish regions. The Thursday-to-Sunday break is a time to plan ahead for island travel, so ferries, inter-island flights and rural hotels fill early. Holy Week processions are held in many towns across the islands, and religious services shape the day in historic centres such as San Cristóbal de La Laguna on Tenerife and Vegueta in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria.

Island holidays in 2027

Each island council (cabildo) chooses one holiday, usually for its patron saint. These apply only on that island and replace Santiago Apóstol (25 July), which is not a holiday in the Canary Islands.

Carnival Tuesday is a local holiday in many towns, but not on the same date everywhere: several have their local holiday on 9 February 2027, while Santa Cruz de Tenerife has moved its carnival later and holds the holiday on 23 February. See the Santa Cruz de Tenerife Carnival and the Las Palmas de Gran Canaria Carnival, and Los Indianos on Carnival Monday in Santa Cruz de La Palma.

Long weekends in 2027

  • Thursday 25 to Sunday 28 March: Easter, four days everywhere.
  • Friday 1 to Sunday 3 January: New Year.
  • Saturday 14 to Monday 16 August: Assumption.
  • Saturday 30 October to Monday 1 November: All Saints.
  • Monday 6 and Wednesday 8 December: two holidays in one week, a popular time for a short break.
  • Island extras: Fuerteventura (Friday 17 September), El Hierro (Friday 24 September) and La Gomera (Monday 4 October) each get a long weekend of their own.

Residents of the islands travel between them on these weekends, so book ferries, inter-island flights and rural houses early, especially on the smaller islands. Visitors from the rest of Spain also arrive for the national long weekends.

What closes and what stays open

The official calendar is a labour calendar: it sets paid, non-recoverable days off for employees ("inhábiles para el trabajo, retribuidos y no recuperables" in the decree's words) and non-working days for official deadlines. It does not say which businesses must close, and the decree itself notes that a day being non-working for deadlines does not on its own decide how public offices operate. In practice, what you will notice on a holiday:

  • Government offices and official services: check the office's own opening calendar before planning in-person paperwork.
  • Hotels and airports: check your booking and flight status, including at Tenerife South and Gran Canaria.
  • Buses, ferries and attractions may run reduced or holiday timetables, or change opening hours. Check the operator's own page for the specific date before you set out.
  • Shops, bars and restaurants have their own opening calendars. Expect more to be open in resort areas than in residential towns, but do not count on a particular business opening on 1 January, Good Friday or 25 December.

For holiday planning across the year, see the best time to visit the Canary Islands and our winter guide, and for everyday practicalities, local tips.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many public holidays do the Canary Islands have in 2027?

Eleven holidays apply across the whole archipelago in 2027, plus one island holiday on each island and two local holidays in each municipality, so most workers have 14 days in total.

Is Canary Islands Day a holiday in 2027?

30 May 2027 is a Sunday. The regional decree does not list it as a working holiday for 2027 and does not move it to Monday 31 May, so there is no extra day off. The day is still celebrated.

Are Maundy Thursday and Good Friday holidays in the Canary Islands in 2027?

Yes. Maundy Thursday, 25 March, and Good Friday, 26 March 2027, are both public holidays in the Canary Islands. Easter Monday, 29 March, is not.

Is 15 August a holiday in 2027?

The Assumption falls on Sunday 15 August 2027, so the Canary Islands give the day off on Monday 16 August instead.

What is Tenerife's island holiday in 2027?

Tuesday 2 February 2027, the feast of the Virgen de la Candelaria. It applies only on Tenerife.

Is Carnival Tuesday a public holiday?

Not across the islands, but many municipalities choose it as one of their two local holidays. In 2027 it is 9 February in towns including Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, La Laguna, Arona, Arrecife, Tías and Santa Cruz de La Palma, 16 February in Puerto del Rosario and 23 February in Santa Cruz de Tenerife.

Are shops open on public holidays in the resorts?

Opening varies by business. Check opening hours for shops, attractions and transport on the day itself, especially on 1 January, Good Friday and 25 December.

guides.title: Mount Teide Permit and Cable Car: Tenerife Summit Rules
guides.summary: On Tenerife, Teide National Park is free, the cable car is a paid ticket, and the last stretch to the 3,715 m summit needs its own permit from Tenerife ON.
guides.html:
Mount Teide, in the centre of Tenerife, is the highest point in Spain, and three separate things control how close you get to the top. The Teide National Park is open to drive into without a ticket. The Teide cable car is a private, paid service that lifts you to La Rambleta, about 160 metres below the summit. The final path from La Rambleta to the crater rim is a third matter: it needs its own permit, booked through the Cabildo de Tenerife's Tenerife ON platform, and a cable car ticket does not include it.

Rules and prices below come from the Cabildo de Tenerife, the Teide cable car operator (volcanoteide.com) and the national parks booking site as read in November 2026. Where we could not open an official page, we say so. Rules have changed often since 2024: check Tenerife ON before you travel.

Park, cable car and summit: three different things

WhatWho runs itCostBooking
Teide National Park (roads, viewpoints, visitor centres)Cabildo de TenerifeNo entry ticket for the park itselfNone to drive in
Teide cable car to La Rambleta (about 3,555 m)Teleférico del Pico del Teide (volcanoteide.com)Paid ticketTimed tickets online
Telesforo Bravo path, La Rambleta to the summit (3,715 m)Cabildo de TenerifeFree for Tenerife residents; a fee in chargeable hours for other visitors aged 14 and over since January 2026Permit on Tenerife ON, by day and time slot

The park was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2007 and covers about 19,000 hectares, according to the island's tourism board. Roads in are the TF-21, TF-24 and TF-38. As of November 2026, the El Portillo and Cañada Blanca visitor centres are open 9 am to 4 pm, closed on 25 December and 1 January. Many people come only for the drive, the lava fields and the night sky, and need no permit.

The Teide cable car

The cable car runs from a base station at 2,356 metres to La Rambleta at 3,555 metres, a ride of about eight minutes according to the operator. As of November 2026 return tickets start at 43 euros for a non-resident adult and 21.50 euros for a non-resident child aged 3 to 13; one-way tickets are 24 euros for adults. Canary Islands residents pay less. From 25 October to 31 December 2026 the published hours are 9 am to 5 pm, with the last ascent at 4 pm and the last descent at 4.50 pm. Summer hours run later.

The operator's rules:

  • Who cannot ride. People with cardiovascular conditions, pregnant women and children under 3 are not allowed on the cable car because of the altitude. Children under 16 must be with an adult at all times.
  • Descent tickets. If you walk up and want to ride down, the descent ticket can only be bought at the upper station, by QR code, and only if the cable car is running.
  • Ascent-only tickets. Anyone planning to walk down a trail that needs authorisation (PNT 07, 09, 23 or 28) is refused an ascent-only ticket without that permit.

The cable car stops in high wind, ice or for technical reasons, sometimes at short notice. As of November 2026, the operator's terms provide a full refund if weather or technical reasons prevent the cable-car activity. If the cable car runs but the summit trails are closed, a cable-car-only ticket remains valid and is not refundable on that basis.

Without a summit permit you can still walk the two short viewpoint trails from La Rambleta when the authority has opened them, towards La Fortaleza and towards Pico Viejo, whose crater sits at 3,104 metres.

The summit permit: Telesforo Bravo trail (PNT 10)

The Telesforo Bravo path is the only way to the summit. It is an out-and-back trail from La Rambleta to the Pico del Teide, 0.69 km long and taking about 45 minutes according to the island's tourism board, with gradients of up to 60%. The Cabildo de Tenerife's access rules of October 2025 moved bookings from the national parks reservation site to Tenerife ON (tenerifeon.es and its app), the Cabildo's own platform. The national parks site (reservasparquesnacionales.es) now simply points visitors there.

The October 2025 access rules remain useful background, but the Cabildo announced revised slots in October 2026. As of November 2026, use the conditions and slot on your Tenerife ON permit:

  • Time slots. The Cabildo's October 2026 announcement changes the summit visits from two-hour to 90-minute intervals, including revised sunrise access. Go by the slot printed on your permit.
  • Numbers. Places are limited and allocated across visitor categories, including accredited guides and federation members. Check the live availability for your category.
  • Group size and frequency. Enter every participant when booking and check the current group and repeat-booking limits on Tenerife ON. The one-per-week rule was in the October 2025 resolution; we could not verify the current limit.
  • Identity. Carry the permit on paper or on your phone together with an official ID (passport or national identity card) for every person named on it. If anyone refuses to show them, or the names do not match, the permit is cancelled.
  • Leave on time. The permit is valid only for the people, day and slot on it, and you must leave the trail when your slot ends.
  • No-shows. People who hold a permit and do not use it, without good reason, can be barred from applying for three months.
  • Age. No access for children under 3; under-16s must be with an adult.
  • Not linked to the cable car. The permit is valid for its day and slot whether or not the cable car runs that day. If it stops, you walk down.

When to book. Check Tenerife ON early and use its live reservation calendar. We could not verify the current booking-release window on the platform, so do not rely on older advice to book more than three months ahead. Some guided tours include a permit: check the particular tour before paying.

Fees. The Cabildo began charging for the Telesforo Bravo and Montaña Blanca trails on 19 January 2026 in chargeable hours for visitors who are not residents of Tenerife, with exemptions; Tenerife residents remain free. As of November 2026, the Cabildo's October announcement lists PNT 10 at 15 euros for visitors resident outside the Canary Islands and 6 euros for residents of the other Canary Islands; under-14s are exempt. For PNT 07, visitors resident outside the Canary Islands pay 6 euros on weekdays or 10 euros on Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays; residents of the other islands pay 3 or 5 euros respectively. Tenerife residents pay nothing. The Cabildo's October announcement places chargeable hours at 9 am to 6 pm, while the text of its October resolution gives 09:00 to 17:00, so treat late-afternoon slots as chargeable unless Tenerife ON shows otherwise. Check your category and final price on Tenerife ON. Note that some older official pages, including the island tourism board's park page, still describe the permit as free.

Walking up: Montaña Blanca (PNT 07) and the Altavista refuge

The classic hike starts at Montaña Blanca, beside the TF-21, at 2,348 metres. The island tourism board describes the PNT 07 Montaña Blanca to La Rambleta trail as a linear route of 8.2 km taking about five and a half hours, and highly challenging because of the climb and the altitude. It needs a Tenerife ON booking of its own, and since January 2026 it carries a fee for visitors who are not Tenerife residents. Getting from La Rambleta to the summit still needs the separate PNT 10 permit. Since November 2024 authorisation has also been needed for other park trails, including PNT 09 and PNT 23, and part of PNT 28.

The Refugio de Altavista, at 3,260 metres, is the only mountain refuge in the park and can be reached only on foot. The operator's live status page showed it as open when checked in November 2026; check again before setting out. As of November 2026 a standard overnight stay starts at 71 euros (with lower rates for Tenerife residents and FEDME mountaineering federation members) and includes a bunk in a shared dormitory, a Montaña Blanca trail permit, and access to the summit path between 6 am and 7.30 am the next morning, early enough for sunrise from the top. The refuge's own FAQ gives a slightly different summit window, so check your booking confirmation. Check-in is from 7 pm to 10 pm, guests must leave their rooms by 8 am, and the stay is for ages 14 and over. You must bring a sleeping bag and your own food.

For more on routes and timing, see our climbing Mount Teide page and the wider hiking in the Canary Islands guide.

Other trail rules on Teide

The Cabildo's own announcement of 14 October 2026 confirms reservations for PNT 09, PNT 23 and PNT 28. As of November 2026, it lists daily quotas of 95, 65 and 65 respectively, with no trail fee for these three routes. Compulsory equipment includes long trousers, warm clothing, mountain boots, a charged phone, an emergency thermal blanket, water, a hat, gloves and a torch or head torch with spare batteries. Staff can refuse access without the equipment even if you have a reservation. Entering without authorisation can attract fines of up to 600 euros. Check the trail conditions on Tenerife ON before travelling. The October 2025 rules already allow park staff to refuse access to anyone without the compulsory equipment.

Leaving the marked path, walking around the crater rim and entering the crater are all prohibited, because the crater is a reserve zone. Pets are not allowed on the summit path, except guide dogs.

Altitude, cold and winter ice

The Cabildo's rules describe the Telesforo Bravo as a high-mountain trail unsuitable for people with heart, breathing or mobility problems, or without high-mountain experience, with steep slopes, loose ground and places where a fall is possible. They warn of sudden temperature changes and low oxygen that can cause extreme tiredness, dizziness and general sickness. In practice:

  • Altitude. The cable car climbs from 2,356 to 3,555 metres in about eight minutes, after you have already travelled up from the coast. Walk slowly, drink water and turn back if you get a headache, nausea or dizziness.
  • Cold. The island tourism board warns that summit temperatures can drop several degrees below zero even in summer. Bring warm layers, a hat, gloves and a windproof jacket, even if the coast is 25 degrees.
  • Winter ice and snow. In winter Teide often carries snow and ice (see the Canary Islands in winter). The Cabildo can close the Telesforo Bravo, including for people who already have permits, because of ice or snow. Once the worst weather passes but ice remains, access may be limited to experienced mountaineers who book a specific permit and declare they have the training and equipment.

In an emergency call 112. See our emergency contacts page and check the weather the day before; the best time to visit guide explains the seasons.

Planning a Teide day

Most visitors drive up from the south coast resorts of Costa Adeje and Los Cristianos, or from Puerto de la Cruz in the north through the Orotava Valley. Allow a full day: check the cable-car parking arrangements before setting out. Combine the park with the cliffs of Los Gigantes or the village of Masca on the way back west, or with La Laguna to the north-east. Our Tenerife 7-day itinerary, things to do in Tenerife and where to stay in Tenerife fit Teide into a wider trip, and our local tips cover driving and etiquette. The volcano and lava tube page covers volcanic sights on other islands too, including Timanfaya on Lanzarote.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do you need a permit to go up Mount Teide?

Not to enter Teide National Park or to ride the cable car to La Rambleta. You do need a separate permit, booked on the Cabildo de Tenerife's Tenerife ON platform, to walk the Telesforo Bravo path from La Rambleta to the summit. Walking up from Montaña Blanca needs its own booking as well.

Is the Teide summit permit free?

It is free for residents of Tenerife. Since 19 January 2026 the Cabildo has charged other visitors for the Telesforo Bravo and Montaña Blanca trails. As of November 2026, PNT 10 costs 15 euros for visitors resident outside the Canary Islands or 6 euros for residents of the other islands in chargeable hours; under-14s are exempt. Check the final price on Tenerife ON.

How far in advance should I book the Teide summit permit?

As early as you can. Use the current Tenerife ON booking calendar. Some guided tours and overnight refuge bookings include permits, subject to availability and their own conditions.

Does the cable car ticket include the summit?

No. The cable car takes you to La Rambleta at 3,555 metres. The last stretch to the 3,715-metre summit needs the separate Telesforo Bravo permit.

Can children climb Teide?

Children under 3 are not allowed on the cable car or the summit path, and under-16s must be with an adult. The Altavista refuge accepts guests aged 14 and over.

Is the Altavista refuge open?

The operator's live status page showed it as open when checked in November 2026; check again before setting out. The refuge sits at 3,260 metres, is reached only on foot, and a stay includes access to the summit path early the next morning. It can close for weather, in which case bookings can be changed or cancelled free of charge.

Can you climb Teide in winter?

Sometimes, but snow and ice are common in winter and the Cabildo closes the summit path when conditions are dangerous, even for permit holders. When ice remains after a storm, access may be limited to experienced mountaineers with the right equipment.

guides.title: Things to Do in Fuerteventura: A Guide by Interest
guides.summary: Things to do in Fuerteventura start with the Corralejo dunes, Isla de Lobos (free permit, capped visits), Cofete's empty beach and the old capital, Betancuria.
guides.html:
Fuerteventura is the long, dry island in the east of the Canary Islands, in the province of Las Palmas. It is a beach and wind island first: the coast is lined with pale sand, and the steady trade winds draw windsurfers and kitesurfers from all over Europe. Inland, the landscape is bare brown hills, old volcanoes and a handful of quiet villages. UNESCO lists the island as a Biosphere Reserve. Flights arrive at Fuerteventura Airport (FUE) near Puerto del Rosario, in the middle of the east coast; the main bases are Corralejo in the north and the Jandía peninsula in the south. The Fuerteventura island guide covers the basics; this guide is arranged by interest.

Landscapes and parks

Just south of Corralejo, the Corralejo Dunes Natural Park is a sea of white sand running down to the beaches, with the main road cutting through it. Walk into the dunes for a view away from town. Keep off the vegetation that holds the sand together and take water, as shade is scarce.

A short drive inland, Calderón Hondo is a volcano near Lajares with a well-marked path up to the rim, where you look straight down into a deep, round crater. On the west coast, the Ajuy caves are large sea caves reached on a cliff path from the black-sand beach and fishing village of Ajuy; the layered cliffs are worth a look even if geology is not your thing. Keep well back from the edge in rough seas.

In the far south-west, behind the Jandía mountains, Playa de Cofete is one of the wildest beaches in the Canary Islands: kilometres of sand under a wall of mountains, with almost nothing built on it. You reach it on an unpaved mountain track from the Morro Jable side. Drive slowly, check whether your hire car contract allows unpaved roads, and carry water and food, rather than relying on beach facilities.

Beaches

The Grandes Playas de Corralejo run along the edge of the dunes, wide and pale, with Isla de Lobos and Lanzarote on the horizon. On the south-east coast of Jandía, Playa de Sotavento is a long beach with a tidal lagoon that fills and empties with the tide, famous for kitesurfing and windsurfing. On the north-west coast, El Cotillo has the Playa de La Concha and the El Cotillo lagoons, rock-sheltered pools of turquoise water that are some of the calmest swimming on the island.

Cofete is for looking at, not swimming: the open Atlantic there has strong currents and heavy surf. The best beaches in the Canary Islands guide compares these with the other islands.

Towns and culture

Betancuria, in a valley in the western hills, was founded at the beginning of the 15th century by the Norman Jean de Béthencourt and stayed the island's capital until 1834. Its church of Santa María, whitewashed streets and small museums make a calm half day, and the road there over the mountains has wide viewpoints. Corralejo is a resort town, with a harbour, bars and restaurants; El Cotillo, in the north-west, is a fishing village with a laid-back surf scene.

The island's best-known product is queso majorero, goat's cheese often rubbed with paprika or gofio. Order it with papas arrugadas and mojo picón, and try gofio in one of its many forms.

On the water

Wind is the island's main resource for sport. Sotavento's lagoon in the south and the beaches around Corralejo in the north are the main spots for windsurfing and kitesurfing. The north and west coasts have reef breaks and beach breaks for surfing, from schools for beginners to heavy waves for experts. For calmer water, the El Cotillo lagoons and the sheltered bay on Isla de Lobos suit snorkelling, and dive centres in the north and the south run trips for scuba diving. Once a year, the Fuerteventura kite festival fills the sky over the Corralejo dunes with giant kites.

Isla de Lobos

Isla de Lobos is a small, uninhabited volcanic island off Corralejo, protected as a natural park (Parque Natural Islote de Lobos). Boats from Corralejo harbour make the short crossing. On the island, a marked trail loops round the coast and a path climbs its small volcano for a view back to Fuerteventura and across to Lanzarote.

The rule that matters: you need an authorisation to land, issued free of charge by the Cabildo de Fuerteventura (the island council) through its official LobosPass website, lobospass.com. You choose a date and a visiting shift, and each shift has a capped number of places, shown as availability when you book; in busy periods the shifts fill up. As of November 2026, check whether your boat operator arranges the authorisation or whether you need to request it yourself. The Cabildo permit is free; check what any extra charge covers. Take water, food, sun protection and your own rubbish back with you: there are almost no services on the island.

Walks

Fuerteventura's hiking is about volcanic cones, ridges and coast rather than forest. Calderón Hondo has an accessible walking route; the full circuit around Isla de Lobos is a walk of several kilometres; the hills around Betancuria have longer paths with big views. In the south, the Jandía mountains above Cofete are wild and steep. Start early: there is almost no shade and the wind can be tiring.

With children

The El Cotillo lagoons and the town beaches in Corralejo are the easiest swims for children. Running down the dunes is free entertainment, and a boat trip to Isla de Lobos feels like a proper adventure if you book the authorisation ahead. Avoid Cofete and the exposed west-coast beaches for swimming. The kite festival is a good family day out if your dates match.

A windy or cloudy day

Expect wind: it is what Fuerteventura is famous for. On a day when the beach is too blowy, head inland to Betancuria and its viewpoints, add the Ajuy caves if the sea is calm, and stop for cheese and coffee in a village. On the south of Jandía, the leeward side of the peninsula can be more sheltered than the north. Check Canary Islands weather before choosing a beach.

A day trip by ferry

From Corralejo, ferries cross the strait to Playa Blanca in the south of Lanzarote; Fred. Olsen Express lists the crossing at 25 or 35 minutes depending on the vessel, and Líneas Romero gives about 30 minutes, as of November 2026. A day there could take in the Papagayo beaches or, with a hire car, Timanfaya National Park. From Morro Jable in the south, Fred. Olsen sails to Las Palmas on Gran Canaria in about 2 hours, better for a change of base than a day out. Read island hopping by ferry and plane for the options, and things to do in Lanzarote if the day trip turns into a longer stay. If you are combining two or three islands, the two-week island-hopping itinerary shows how the ferries fit together.

What Fuerteventura is not good for

Fuerteventura is not the island for green landscapes, mountain forests or a dense calendar of museums and architecture; Tenerife, La Palma and La Gomera do those better, and Lanzarote has more to see in a day. It is long and thinly populated, so allow plenty of time for a trip from Corralejo to Cofete. Public transport to remote beaches is limited, but TIADHE lists Line 111 between Morro Jable, Cofete and Punta de Jandía; check the current timetable and return service before setting out. The wind that sailors love can sandblast a beach towel in the afternoon, especially in summer. Nightlife is concentrated in Corralejo. If you are still choosing an island, read which Canary Island is best.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do you need a permit to visit Isla de Lobos?

Yes. To land on Isla de Lobos you need an authorisation from the Cabildo de Fuerteventura, issued free through its LobosPass website for a chosen date and visiting shift, with a limited number of places per shift. Some boat tickets include it and some do not, so check when you book.

How do you get to Playa de Cofete?

By an unpaved mountain track from the Morro Jable side of the Jandía peninsula. Drive slowly, check your car hire terms for unpaved roads, and take water and food, rather than relying on beach facilities. Do not swim there: currents are strong.

Is Fuerteventura too windy for a beach holiday?

Not if you choose your beach. The wind is steady for much of the year, but sheltered spots such as the El Cotillo lagoons and the leeward side of Jandía are calmer, and the wind keeps the heat comfortable. Sailors and kiters come for exactly that wind.

How many days do you need in Fuerteventura?

Five days lets you see the north (dunes, Lobos, El Cotillo), the centre (Betancuria, Ajuy) and the south (Sotavento, Cofete) without rushing. Our Fuerteventura 5-day itinerary shows one route.

Can you visit Lanzarote from Fuerteventura in a day?

Yes. Ferries from Corralejo reach Playa Blanca in Lanzarote in about 25 to 35 minutes, so a day trip to the Papagayo beaches or Timanfaya is easy to fit in.

Pick your threads, perhaps dunes and Lobos in the north or wind and wild beaches in the south, and Fuerteventura gives you space and sand that the busier islands cannot match.
guides.bestTime: All year; choose walking days according to local conditions
guides.budget: Low to moderate: beaches, dunes, walks and the Lobos permit are free; car hire, boats and water sports are the main costs
