guides.title: Things to Do in Gran Canaria: A Guide by Interest
guides.summary: Things to do in Gran Canaria range from the Maspalomas dunes and a booked walk to Roque Nublo to Vegueta, Las Canteras, Puerto de Mogán and the Agaete ferry.
guides.html:
Gran Canaria is the round island in the middle of the Canary Islands, in the province of Las Palmas. It packs three very different trips into one: a resort coast in the south around Maspalomas, a mountain interior of pine woods, ravines and stone villages, and a working capital in the north-east, Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, with its own city beach. Most visitors land at Gran Canaria Airport (LPA) on the east coast, roughly halfway between the two. This guide is arranged by interest, so you can pick the threads that suit you; the Gran Canaria island guide covers the basics of getting around.

Landscapes and parks

The Maspalomas dunes are the island's best-known landscape: a field of golden sand between Playa del Inglés and Maspalomas, running down to the sea next to a lighthouse that has stood there since 1890. The dunes are a protected nature reserve, so keep to the marked paths rather than climbing wherever you like. Go early in the morning or late in the afternoon, when the sand is cooler and the ridges throw long shadows.

Inland, the road climbs from the coast into the centre of the island around Tejeda. Here the landmark is Roque Nublo, a volcanic monolith on a high ridge that the island uses as its emblem. Access has changed: as of November 2026 the Cabildo de Gran Canaria (the island council) uses a booking system for regulated visiting slots, reached through its trails website, grancanariasenderos.com, or reservasroquenublo.com. Check the current slots and exemptions before setting out. Use designated car parks and reach the monument by shuttle bus or on foot along the summit trails. Do not plan on parking at the trailhead the way older guides describe. The walk up is short but steep and stony, so wear proper shoes. The official rules require suitable footwear, warm clothing, drinking water and a fully charged mobile phone.

The high centre is also one of the best places on the island to look at the night sky once the coastal haze is below you; see stargazing in the Canary Islands for how to plan it. Cyclists come for the long climbs from the south coast to the summit area, covered in cycling.

Beaches

The south has the sunniest, most reliable beach weather. Playa de Maspalomas runs along the foot of the dunes and feels open and natural. Next to it, Playa del Inglés is the busy resort beach, backed by hotels and promenades. Further west, Playa de Amadores is a man-made crescent of pale sand protected by breakwaters, with calm water that suits weak swimmers.

In the capital, Playa de las Canteras is a city beach that locals use every day. Its secret is La Barra, a long sandstone barrier offshore that shelters much of the beach from the Atlantic swell, so at low tide the water inside is calm and clear enough for snorkelling with a mask straight from the sand.

For something wild, Playa de Güigüí on the west coast has no road at all. You reach it on a long, hot hike over the mountains or by boat, and you should carry all your water and food. It is a full-day commitment, not a quick swim. The best beaches in the Canary Islands guide compares these with beaches on the other islands.

Towns and culture

Start in Vegueta, the old quarter of Las Palmas, whose narrow streets have been the core of the city for more than 500 years. The Casa de Colón, a museum of history and art, is the anchor of a slow morning around the cathedral square and the side streets. During Carnival, the Las Palmas de Gran Canaria Carnival takes over the city with parades and late-night street parties.

In the south-west, Puerto de Mogán is a small harbour village of whitewashed houses, bougainvillea and narrow canals, with cafés along the marina. It is pretty and popular, so arrive in the morning or stay for the evening rather than visiting at midday.

On the north-west coast, Agaete and its harbour, Puerto de las Nieves, are where many islanders go for a long Sunday lunch of fresh fish. The harbour has natural rock pools for swimming and sunsets behind the cliffs. If you are on the island on 4 August, the Bajada de la Rama fills Agaete with music and dancers carrying branches down to the sea. Inland, the hill town of Teror, with its basilica and wooden balconies, is an easy stop on the way back to Las Palmas.

Food is part of the culture. Try papas arrugadas with mojo picón, a bowl of sancocho canario (salt fish with potatoes) and a spoonful of gofio, the toasted grain flour that turns up in everything from soups to desserts.

On the water

The trade winds make Gran Canaria a destination for windsurfing and kitesurfing, especially on the windier east coast. Surfers use the reefs and point breaks along the north coast and the stretch of Las Canteras beyond the shelter of La Barra; start with surfing in the Canary Islands for the level each spot suits.

Under the water, the island has volcanic reefs, arches and wrecks for scuba diving, and Las Canteras is the easiest place for snorkelling without a boat. Boat trips from the south-coast marinas go out looking for dolphins and whales; read whale and dolphin watching before you book, so you choose an operator that keeps its distance from the animals.

Walks

Gran Canaria's interior is criss-crossed by old stone paths, the caminos reales, that once linked the villages before roads arrived. The walks around Tejeda and the Roque Nublo ridge give the biggest views for the effort; longer routes link the summit area with the coast through pine forest and ravines. Our hiking page covers route planning, water and the difference between a shaded northern trail and an exposed southern one. If you like your walking at race pace, the Transgrancanaria ultra-trail crosses the island every year.

The weather in the mountains can be very different from the beach: cooler, windier and sometimes wrapped in cloud. Pack a layer even when the coast is hot.

With children

For families, the calm water at Amadores and inside the reef at Las Canteras is easier than the open beaches. A short walk on the marked paths into the Maspalomas dunes feels like a desert adventure without going far from the car; take water and hats. Puerto de Mogán's canals and harbour boats keep younger children interested, and the rock pools at Puerto de las Nieves in Agaete are good for crab-spotting. Leave Güigüí and the long mountain hikes for older children who already walk well.

A windy or cloudy day

The north of the island catches more cloud than the south, and the trade winds can make the east coast blustery. On a grey day, head for the capital: Vegueta and the Casa de Colón are at their best without a beach to compete with, and the city's shopping streets and markets fill the rest of the day. Teror and the botanical garden near Las Palmas (Jardín Canario) also work well under cloud. If the north is grey, the south is often sunny, so driving from one to the other is a fair plan B. Check Canary Islands weather before you set off.

A day trip by ferry

From Agaete, the Fred. Olsen Express fast ferry crosses to Santa Cruz de Tenerife; the operator lists the crossing at 80 minutes as of November 2026 and runs a free ferry bus between central Las Palmas and the port at Agaete for its passengers. Book a bus seat in advance, as places are limited. That makes a day on Tenerife realistic, for example for La Laguna's old town and the Anaga Rural Park close to the port. The same company sails from the port of Las Palmas to Morro Jable in the south of Fuerteventura in about 2 hours, which suits a longer stay more than a day trip; see things to do in Fuerteventura if you go. The island hopping by ferry and plane page and the island-hopping guide compare routes and operators.

What Gran Canaria is not good for

Gran Canaria is not a quiet island everywhere. The south coast between Playa del Inglés and Meloneras is heavily built up, and if you want empty villages and dark nights the smaller western islands such as La Gomera or El Hierro suit you better. The interior roads are winding and slow, so distances on the map take longer than you expect. Roque Nublo has regulated booking slots and requires a bus or walk from designated parking, so it is not a spur-of-the-moment stop. In winter, the sea is cooler than many visitors expect and the north can be cloudy for days; read the Canary Islands in winter if you are coming for guaranteed heat. If you are still choosing an island, start with which Canary Island is best.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many days do you need for Gran Canaria?

Five to seven days lets you combine beach time in the south with a day in the mountains, a day in Las Palmas and an afternoon in Agaete or Puerto de Mogán. Our Gran Canaria 7-day itinerary sets out one way to do it.

Do you need to book to visit Roque Nublo?

For regulated visiting slots, yes. As of November 2026 use the booking system linked from grancanariasenderos.com, at reservasroquenublo.com. Use designated parking and continue by shuttle bus or on foot. Check the booking page for current slots and exemptions before you go.

Is Las Canteras good for swimming?

Yes, for most of its length. La Barra, the reef offshore, shelters a large part of the beach from the swell, so the water inside is usually calm. The section outside the reef's shelter gets waves and is used by surfers.

Can you visit Tenerife in a day from Gran Canaria?

Yes. The fast ferry from Agaete to Santa Cruz de Tenerife takes about 80 minutes, and the operator runs a free ferry bus from central Las Palmas to Agaete for its passengers. Reserve the ferry bus in advance and check the return time before you plan the day.

Do you need a car on Gran Canaria?

Not for the coast and the capital, which the island's bus network serves. For the mountain villages, Güigüí's trailheads and flexible days in the interior, a hire car makes life much easier. See getting around the Canary Islands for buses, car hire and taxis.

Pick two or three threads, perhaps dunes and beaches, mountains and villages, or the capital and its city beach, and Gran Canaria rewards a week far more than the resort strip alone suggests.
guides.bestTime: All year in the south; check mountain conditions before walking
guides.budget: Low to moderate: beaches, dunes, walks and Vegueta are free; car hire and ferries are the main costs

guides.title: Things to Do in Lanzarote: A Guide by Interest
guides.summary: Things to do in Lanzarote centre on Timanfaya's 1730 to 1736 lava fields, César Manrique sites, Papagayo's coves and the short ferry from Órzola to La Graciosa.
guides.html:
Lanzarote is the north-eastern island of the Canary Islands, in the province of Las Palmas, with extensive volcanic landscapes. Black lava fields, red cones and white villages make it look like nowhere else in the archipelago, and the artist César Manrique turned several of its caves, cliffs and quarries into places you can visit. UNESCO declared the whole island a Biosphere Reserve, towns included. You will land at Lanzarote Airport (ACE) near Arrecife; most visitors stay in Puerto del Carmen or Playa Blanca. The Lanzarote island guide covers the basics; this guide is arranged by interest.

Landscapes and parks

Timanfaya National Park protects more than 5,100 hectares of lava left by six years of eruptions between 1730 and 1736. You cannot roam freely across its core. The standard visit is the Montañas del Fuego (Fire Mountains) centre on the Islote de Hilario, where a coach takes you along the Ruta de los Volcanes, a road of about 14 kilometres that Manrique laid out through the craters. As of November 2026 the ticket costs €30 (children up to 6 free), the centre opens 09:00 to 15:45 every day, and tickets are sold online only, for a fixed date and time. The ticket includes the 35-minute coach route and the geothermal demonstrations, where staff show how hot the ground still is a few metres down. The El Diablo restaurant grills food over a well of volcanic heat; it takes no reservations.

East of the park, La Geria is the island's wine country: vines planted in hollows dug through the volcanic ash, each sheltered by a curved stone wall. It is a striking drive, and several bodegas along the road offer wine tasting. On the west coast near El Golfo, the green lagoon (Charco de los Clicos) sits inside a half-eroded crater beside a black beach; you look at it from the path above rather than swim in it.

For the island's volcanic tubes and craters as a whole, see volcano and lava tube visits.

The César Manrique sites

Manrique's work is the main reason Lanzarote feels different from its neighbours. The island's art, culture and tourism centres (CACT) run several sites associated with his work, while Cueva de los Verdes was adapted by Jesús Soto. Manrique's foundation runs his former home. Prices and hours below are as of November 2026.

  • Jameos del Agua: the first centre Manrique created, inside a collapsed section of a lava tube from the La Corona volcano, with a saltwater lake and an underground auditorium. From €17, 10:00 to 18:00.
  • Cueva de los Verdes: a guided walk of about one kilometre through levels of the same lava tube, in Spanish and English. €17, 09:30 to 16:45, booked online for a set time.
  • Mirador del Río: a viewpoint built into the top of the northern cliffs, with windows facing La Graciosa across the strait. €9, 10:00 to 17:00, last entry 16:40.
  • Jardín de Cactus: a garden in a former quarry at Guatiza, with terraces of cacti from five continents. €9, 10:00 to 17:00.
  • Fundación César Manrique: Manrique's former home at Tahíche, built into a lava flow, now a gallery. €10 standard, 10:00 to 17:30, ticket desk closes 17:00. His house museum in Haría is also open, at the same price, from 10:30 to 17:30, with its ticket desk closing at 17:00. Both museums close on 1 January.

Children aged 0 to 6 enter the CACT centres free. Book the two timed sites (Montañas del Fuego and Cueva de los Verdes) first and build the rest of the day around them.

Beaches

In the far south, the Playas de Papagayo are a string of sandy coves below low cliffs, reached by a dirt track through the protected Los Ajaches area. They are close to Playa Blanca and offer sheltered swimming in calm conditions. As of November 2026, the Ayuntamiento de Yaiza lists a €3 entrance charge to Los Ajaches for non-residents of Lanzarote, payable by card only. In Puerto del Carmen, Playa Grande is the main resort beach, with a promenade behind it.

On the north-west coast, Playa de Famara is a long, wild beach under the Risco de Famara cliffs. It is superb for walking and surfing and dangerous for casual swimming: currents are strong and waves break hard. In the north-east, near Órzola, Caletón Blanco has white sand and shallow lagoons between black lava, which children love at low tide. For more, read the best beaches in the Canary Islands.

Towns and culture

Teguise, the old capital, has cobbled streets, churches and low whitewashed houses, and has a historic centre worth exploring. Haría, in the north, sits in a valley of palm trees and holds Manrique's house museum. Arrecife, the capital, is a working town with a lagoon in the middle, worth an hour if you are passing. At the table, look for papas arrugadas with mojo, fresh fish, goat's cheese and the local Malvasía wine from La Geria.

On the water

Famara is a base for surf lessons, and beginners use it on smaller days; start with surfing. Puerto del Carmen is the main base for scuba diving, and the sheltered coves of Papagayo suit snorkelling on calm days. Athletes may recognise the island from the Ironman Lanzarote, whose swim, hilly bike course and run show how windy and steep the island can be.

Walks

Lanzarote is not a mountain island, but it has rewarding hikes: crater rims in the volcanic zone outside the national park, the cliff paths above Famara, and the coast near Órzola. Inside Timanfaya, keep to what the park allows rather than heading out across the lava. The island is popular for road cycling too, though the wind makes every ride harder than its profile suggests. Bring sun protection: there is almost no shade outside the villages.

With children

The Jameos del Agua lake (look for the tiny blind crabs, an endemic species adapted to darkness), the coach ride through Timanfaya and the geothermal demonstrations hold children's attention well. The coves of Papagayo and the lagoons of Caletón Blanco are calmer than the open beaches. Cueva de los Verdes involves low ceilings and dim light, which some young children dislike. Playa Blanca's beaches and promenade are easy with a pushchair.

A windy or cloudy day

Lanzarote is windy much of the year, and some days are grey. That is when the indoor and sheltered sites come into their own: go underground at Cueva de los Verdes and Jameos del Agua, spend a morning at the Manrique foundation in Tahíche and his house in Haría, and finish with a tasting in La Geria. The Jardín de Cactus is walled and partly sheltered. Mirador del Río is best saved for a clear day, since cloud can hide the view of La Graciosa. Check Canary Islands weather first.

A day trip by ferry

La Graciosa, the small island facing the Mirador del Río, is the classic day out. As of November 2026, ferries leave the harbour at Órzola, in the far north, roughly every 30 minutes, and the crossing takes 25 to 30 minutes with Líneas Romero, one of the companies on the route. La Graciosa has no asphalt roads: the village of Caleta de Sebo has streets of sand, and you explore on foot or by bike, which you can hire in the village. Walk or cycle to Playa de las Conchas on the north coast for the view of the volcanic cones, but treat the sea there with respect: currents can be strong. Take water, as facilities are limited away from the villages.

From Playa Blanca, ferries cross the strait to Corralejo in the north of Fuerteventura; Fred. Olsen Express lists 25 or 35 minutes depending on the vessel, as of November 2026. A day there gives you the Corralejo dunes and the town's beaches. The island hopping page compares routes, and things to do in Fuerteventura covers the neighbouring island in depth.

What Lanzarote is not good for

Lanzarote is not green. If you want forests, high mountains and shady trails, La Palma, La Gomera or Tenerife suit you better. Its best sights are spread out and buses do not reach them all on a convenient schedule, so most visitors hire a car. The paid sites add up if you visit all of them, and the wind can make beach days uncomfortable on the exposed north and west coasts. Famara and La Graciosa's northern beaches are for looking at more than for swimming. If you are still choosing, read which Canary Island is best.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many days do you need in Lanzarote?

Four or five days covers Timanfaya, the Manrique sites, a beach day at Papagayo and a day on La Graciosa. Our Lanzarote 5-day itinerary puts them in a sensible order.

Do you need to book Timanfaya in advance?

Yes. As of November 2026 tickets for Montañas del Fuego, the visitor centre where the coach route through Timanfaya starts, are sold online only, for a specific date and time. The general ticket costs €30, and children up to 6 go free.

Which César Manrique site should you see if you only have time for one?

Jameos del Agua shows his idea best: a natural lava cave turned into a lake, garden and concert hall. If you prefer art and architecture to caves, choose the Fundación César Manrique, his former home built into the lava at Tahíche.

How do you get to La Graciosa?

By ferry from Órzola in the north of Lanzarote. As of November 2026, crossings take 25 to 30 minutes and leave roughly every half hour in the day. There are no tarmac roads on the island, so plan to walk or hire a bike in the village.

Can you swim at Playa de Famara?

Do not treat swimming ability as a guarantee of safety. Follow local flags and lifeguard instructions. Famara is exposed to Atlantic swell and has strong currents. Papagayo's coves in the south are more sheltered, but check conditions there too.

Choose two threads, perhaps volcanoes and Manrique or beaches and La Graciosa, and Lanzarote gives you a week of landscapes you will not find anywhere else in Europe.

guides.title: Things to Do in Tenerife: Teide, the North and the Coast
guides.summary: Things to do in Tenerife, Canary Islands, sorted by interest: Teide, the north, the southern resorts, whales, beaches, towns, family days and bad-weather plans.
guides.html:
Tenerife, the largest of the Canary Islands, is two islands in one. The south is dry, sunny and built around resorts; the north is green, cooler and full of old towns and banana terraces. Between them rises Teide, Spain's highest peak, inside a national park you can drive across in an afternoon. This guide groups the best things to do on Tenerife by interest, so you can build days around what you enjoy rather than a checklist. Distances are short enough that most of it works as day trips from any base; our where to stay in Tenerife guide helps you pick one.

Teide and the national park

Teide National Park was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2007, and it is the reason many people choose Tenerife over its neighbours. The road climbs through pine forest into a wide volcanic crater floor of lava flows, pumice and strange rock towers, with the cone of Teide above. Go early: the light is better, the car parks are emptier and the high road is often above the cloud that sits over the coast.

  • Ride the Teide cable car. As of November 2026 the operator says the cabins reach the top in under eight minutes, to an upper station at 3,555 metres, and that the usual stay up there is limited to one hour (up to two hours with a summit permit). It stops in strong wind or ice, so check on the day and have a plan B.
  • Walk to the summit. The final trail to the crater rim needs a separate permit, booked through Tenerife ON. As of November 2026, the Cabildo lists a €15 fee for visitors resident outside the Canary Islands on the summit trail during the charged daytime hours (from 09:00; check the end time on Tenerife ON); children under 14 are exempt. Other high-mountain trails also require reservations, so check every trail in your route. Our Teide permit and cable car guide and the climbing Mount Teide page explain the options.
  • Walk the crater floor. Shorter marked trails loop around the rock formations near the parador and the visitor centres. See hiking in the Canary Islands for more routes.
  • Stay for the stars. The park's altitude and clean air make it a place to try stargazing. Dress for cold: nights up here are far colder than on the beach.

The green north

The north catches the cloud the trade winds bring, which is why it is green, terraced and often a few degrees cooler than the south. It is also where Tenerife feels most like a Canarian place rather than a holiday resort.

  • Puerto de la Cruz and the Orotava Valley. The island's original resort town has a working harbour, a seafront promenade and old streets. Uphill, the town of La Orotava keeps grand balconied houses; it is famous for the flower and sand carpets of Corpus Christi.
  • Anaga Rural Park. A ridge of jagged peaks and laurel forest at the island's northeast tip, with walking trails, tiny hamlets and the black-sand beach of Playa de Benijo at the end of the road.
  • The Drago Milenario in Icod de los Vinos. A huge, ancient dragon tree, one of the island's symbols, in a small town worth a stroll.
  • Masca and the Teno massif. A hamlet clinging to a ravine in the far northwest, reached by one of the island's most dramatic roads. Walking down the Masca ravine is regulated by the island council: the trail must be booked in advance, a boat transfer out from the bottom is compulsory, and, as of November 2026, independent trail visitors must use TITSA route 355 from Santiago del Teide to reach the start. The path can close for safety work or weather, so check the official booking site before you plan around it.

The south coast resorts

The southern resorts cluster around Costa Adeje, Playa de las Américas and Los Cristianos. The resorts run into one another along a long seafront promenade, which makes an easy walk or cycle between beaches, cafés and harbours.

  • Swim at the resort beaches. Playa del Duque in Costa Adeje has pale sand and a seafront promenade. Check the flags before swimming.
  • See the Los Gigantes cliffs. Sheer walls of rock drop straight into the sea on the west coast. They can be seen from the sea; check the route before booking a boat trip.
  • Get on or under the water. The calm southwest coast suits snorkelling and scuba diving; Playa de las Américas has reef breaks for surfing.
  • Play a round. Several courses sit in the south; see golf in the Canary Islands.
  • Take the ferry to La Gomera. From the port at Los Cristianos, Fred. Olsen lists a 50-minute crossing to San Sebastián de La Gomera as of November 2026, making a day among the forests of Garajonay realistic. The island-hopping guide covers the details.

Whales and dolphins

The stretch of sea between southwest Tenerife and La Gomera was the first place in Europe to be named a Whale Heritage Site, a certification for responsible watching. The island's tourism board lists short-finned pilot whales and bottlenose dolphins as residents, so sightings are likely all year, while other species pass through seasonally. Trips leave from the harbours of Los Cristianos, Costa Adeje and Los Gigantes. Choose a boat with official authorisation for whale watching, expect the skipper to keep a respectful distance, and read our whale and dolphin watching page before you book.

Beaches

Tenerife's natural beaches are mostly dark volcanic sand, with a few golden ones. Pick by mood and by wind.

  • Playa de las Teresitas. A long golden beach near San Andrés, just north of Santa Cruz, protected by a breakwater and popular with local families at weekends.
  • El Médano. A natural sandy bay in the southeast, near the airport. The steady wind makes it a centre for windsurfing and kitesurfing; sunbathers may find it breezy.
  • Playa Jardín. A black-sand beach in Puerto de la Cruz with gardens behind it. The Atlantic swell on the north coast can be strong, so watch the flags.
  • Playa de Benijo. Wild and beautiful in Anaga, better for a walk and a sunset than a swim when the sea is up.

For the full ranking across all the islands, see the best beaches in the Canary Islands.

Towns and culture

  • San Cristóbal de La Laguna. The old town has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1999, and its grid of streets served as a model for colonial cities in the Americas. It is a university town, so it is lively in term time, and largely pedestrian.
  • Santa Cruz de Tenerife. The capital has the white, wave-shaped Auditorio de Tenerife on its waterfront, parks, markets and a tram up to La Laguna. Before Lent the streets fill for the island's biggest party, the Santa Cruz de Tenerife Carnival.
  • Eat Canarian food. Order papas arrugadas with red and green mojo, try conejo en salmorejo in a country restaurant in the north, and finish with a barraquito, a layered coffee served in local cafés. Wine lovers can add wine tasting in the north's vineyards.
  • Time it with a festival. The Three Kings parades on 5 January and Canary Islands Day on 30 May bring the towns out. Check events for the year.

Tenerife with children

  • Siam Park. The big water park in Costa Adeje is a full day out; buy tickets ahead in busy periods.
  • Loro Parque. The large animal park in Puerto de la Cruz, an easy pairing with an afternoon on the north coast.
  • A whale-watching trip. Short trips suit younger children; pick calm-sea mornings.
  • Calm beaches. Consider Playa del Duque and the beaches of Los Cristianos, checking the flags and conditions before paddling.
  • Teide. As of November 2026, children under three are not allowed on the cable car. The operator also excludes pregnant women and people with heart problems. Remember the thin air and cold at the top, and check for weather closures.

The seven-day Tenerife itinerary shows how to mix these with quieter days.

Rainy or windy days

Bad weather on Tenerife is usually local. Cloud and drizzle in the north often mean sun in the south, and the reverse happens when weather comes from the south. Check our weather page, then:

  • Drive to the other side of the island. Check the route, traffic and weather before setting off between north and south.
  • Go indoors in the cities. Santa Cruz has museums and the Auditorio; La Laguna's churches, cafés and covered market fill a wet morning.
  • Visit Loro Parque. Check the forecast and take waterproofs for the outdoor areas.
  • Climb above the cloud. When the coast is grey, Teide is often in sunshine. On windy days the cable car may not run; check road and park closure notices before driving up.
  • Use the wind. A blustery day at El Médano is perfect for watching, or joining, the kitesurfers.

Getting around

A hire car gives the most freedom, especially for Teide, Masca and Anaga. Without one, TITSA buses link the main towns and resorts, and the tram runs between Santa Cruz and La Laguna. For the southern resorts, check flights to Tenerife South, close to the resorts; Tenerife North is next to La Laguna. Read getting around and local tips before you go.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the number one thing to do in Tenerife?

For most visitors it is Teide National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2007. Drive up through the pine forest to the crater floor, ride the cable car if the wind allows, and come back after dark for the stars.

Do I need a permit to climb Mount Teide?

A return cable car ride requires a ticket and compliance with the operator's health restrictions. The short final trail from the upper station to the summit crater needs a separate permit through Tenerife ON. As of November 2026, the Cabildo lists a €15 summit-trail fee for visitors resident outside the Canary Islands in the charged daytime hours from 09:00, with children under 14 exempt. An ascent-only cable car ticket also requires the permits for your descent route. Book ahead. Our Teide permit and cable car guide explains how.

Can you see whales all year in Tenerife?

Yes. Tenerife's tourism board lists short-finned pilot whales and bottlenose dolphins as residents of the waters off the southwest coast, so sightings are likely in any month. Other species are seasonal. Trips leave from Los Cristianos, Costa Adeje and Los Gigantes.

Is the north or the south of Tenerife better for things to do?

They complement each other. The south has the sunniest beaches, the water parks and most boat trips. The north has La Laguna, La Orotava, Puerto de la Cruz, Anaga and Loro Parque. Staying in one and day-tripping to the other is the usual approach.

What can I do in Tenerife when it rains?

Drive to the other side of the island, where the weather is often different, or head up to Teide, which is frequently above the cloud. In the cities, Santa Cruz's museums and the Auditorio and La Laguna's old town work well on a wet day, as does Loro Parque.

Can I visit La Gomera as a day trip from Tenerife?

Yes. Ferries leave from Los Cristianos, and Fred. Olsen lists the crossing to San Sebastián de La Gomera at 50 minutes as of November 2026. A day is enough for Garajonay's forest and a viewpoint or two; staying a night or two is more relaxed.

guides.budget: Moderate; allow for paid attractions, transport and any trail fees

guides.title: Where to Stay in Tenerife: Best Areas by Traveller Type
guides.summary: Pick a Tenerife base by who you travel with, how much sun you need and which airport you land at: the sunny south, the greener north, the cities or the country.
guides.html:
Where you stay on Tenerife decides more than the view from your balcony. It decides how much sun you get, how loud your evenings are, how long your airport transfer takes and if a hire car is essential. The island is big enough that the southern resorts and the northern towns feel like different places, and small enough that you can see both from either. This guide goes area by area, says who each one suits, and explains the one trade-off everybody should understand before booking: south versus north.

The big choice: south or north

Tenerife's mountains split its weather. The northeast trade winds push cloud against the northern slopes, so the north is greener, cooler and more often grey, especially in winter, with more chance of rain. The south and southwest sit in the lee of the mountains, which makes them drier and sunnier, and that is why most of the resorts are there. Neither is wrong.

  • Stay south if reliable sunshine, beach days and easy evenings are the point of the trip.
  • Stay north if you prefer towns with local life, green walking country and a cooler climate, and can live with some cloudy days.
  • Split the stay if you have a week or more: a few nights in each is the best way to see both sides.

Our weather page and best time to visit guide give the detail by season.

Which airport?

Tenerife has two airports, and your base should match the one you land at. Tenerife South (TFS) takes most flights from the UK and Ireland and sits close to the southern resorts. Tenerife North (TFN), beside La Laguna, mainly handles flights to mainland Spain and the other islands. As of November 2026, the airport operator lists TITSA bus lines from Tenerife South to Los Cristianos and Costa Adeje and to Santa Cruz, and a direct bus between the two airports.

Costa Adeje: polished and family-friendly

Costa Adeje is a resort area on the southwest coast, with a long seafront promenade linking its beaches. Playa del Duque is the showpiece, with pale sand and a promenade. Check the flags before swimming. Siam Park is close by, and boat trips for whale and dolphin watching leave from the local harbour. It suits families and couples who want comfort, pools and good restaurants within walking distance. The trade-off is price and a polished feel that has little to do with traditional Canarian life.

Playa de las Américas: for nightlife

Next door, Playa de las Américas is a built-up part of the south known for nightlife. Bars, clubs and late-opening restaurants make it the island's main place for a night out, and its reef breaks draw surfers. It suits groups, younger travellers and anyone who wants everything on the doorstep. Light sleepers should pick a hotel away from the main nightlife streets, or stay in Costa Adeje or Los Cristianos and walk over for the evening.

Los Cristianos: easy and practical

Los Cristianos grew from a fishing village and still has a real town centre, a harbour and a flat seafront that is easy to walk. Check the flags and sea conditions at its beaches. The port is where ferries leave for La Gomera, La Palma and El Hierro; Fred. Olsen lists the crossing to La Gomera at 50 minutes as of November 2026. It suits long winter stays, older travellers, families and anyone planning island hopping. Read the island-hopping guide if you plan a second island.

El Médano: wind and a laid-back village

El Médano, on the southeast coast very close to Tenerife South airport, is a small town with a natural sandy bay and the red cone of Montaña Roja beside it. The near-constant wind makes it one of the best places in the islands for windsurfing and kitesurfing, and it has a younger, more local feel than the big resorts. It suits wind-sports fans, independent travellers and anyone who prefers apartments and cafés to resort hotels. The trade-off is clear: on breezy days, lying on the beach is not much fun.

Los Gigantes and Puerto de Santiago: cliffs and quiet

On the west coast, Los Gigantes and neighbouring Puerto de Santiago sit beneath the Los Gigantes cliffs, which drop straight into the sea. Life centres on a small marina, boat trips along the cliffs, and dark-sand beaches. It is quieter than the main southern resorts while keeping much of their sunshine, and it is a good base for Masca and the Teno hills. It suits couples, walkers and people who want a calmer evening. The streets are steep in places, which matters for anyone with limited mobility.

Puerto de la Cruz: the north's resort town

Puerto de la Cruz is Tenerife's original resort and still its most characterful seaside town, with a harbour, old streets and squares, and the Orotava Valley rising behind it. Playa Jardín is its black-sand beach, Loro Parque is on the edge of town, and the old town of La Orotava is a short drive uphill. It suits travellers who want a real town with local life, walkers heading for the hills, and people who find the south too hot. The trade-off is weather: expect more cloud and some rain, particularly in winter, and a longer transfer from Tenerife South.

La Laguna and Santa Cruz: city bases

San Cristóbal de La Laguna is a UNESCO-listed colonial town and a university city, with pedestrian streets, cafés and bars full of students. Santa Cruz de Tenerife, the capital, has the waterfront Auditorio de Tenerife, shops, markets and the city beach of Playa de las Teresitas a short ride away. A tram links the two. Either works well without a car and puts you close to Tenerife North airport and Anaga Rural Park. They suit culture lovers, food lovers and anyone visiting for the Santa Cruz de Tenerife Carnival. La Laguna sits higher than the coast, so it is cooler and often cloudier than Santa Cruz.

The rural north: casas rurales and walking

The countryside of the north, from the Orotava Valley to the hamlets of Anaga and Teno, has rural houses and small guesthouses rather than resorts. Mornings start with views of Teide or a sea of cloud, and trails start from the door; see hiking. A car helps, nights can be cool, and evenings are quiet. It suits walkers, couples and anyone who wants to see a side of the island most visitors miss. Book with the weather in mind: the high north is where cloud and drizzle are most likely.

How to choose

  • First visit: Costa Adeje or Los Cristianos, with day trips to Teide and the north.
  • Families: Costa Adeje for beaches and Siam Park; Los Cristianos for a flat, walkable town.
  • Nightlife: Playa de las Américas.
  • Couples: Los Gigantes for quiet sunsets, or a rural house in the north.
  • No car: Los Cristianos, Costa Adeje, La Laguna or Santa Cruz, all on good bus or tram routes. See getting around.
  • Winter sun: the southwest coast, from Los Cristianos to Los Gigantes.
  • Culture and food: La Laguna or Puerto de la Cruz.

For ideas on what to do from your base, read things to do in Tenerife and the seven-day Tenerife itinerary. Still choosing an island? Start with which Canary Island is best.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is it better to stay in the north or south of Tenerife?

Stay south for sunshine and beaches: the southern coast sits in the lee of the mountains and is drier and sunnier. Stay north for character, greenery and towns with local life, accepting more cloud and some rain, especially in winter. With a week or more, splitting the stay works well.

Which part of Tenerife is best for families?

Costa Adeje suits most families, with beaches such as Playa del Duque, a long promenade and Siam Park nearby. Los Cristianos is a good alternative, with a flat, walkable seafront, sheltered beaches and a real town centre.

Where should I stay in Tenerife without a car?

Los Cristianos, Costa Adeje, La Laguna and Santa Cruz all work without a car. The southern resorts are linked to Tenerife South airport and to each other by TITSA buses, and the tram connects Santa Cruz with La Laguna.

Which Tenerife airport is closer to the resorts?

Tenerife South is a short drive from Costa Adeje, Playa de las Américas and Los Cristianos, and very close to El Médano. Tenerife North, beside La Laguna, is closer to Santa Cruz, La Laguna and Puerto de la Cruz. Most flights from the UK and Ireland use Tenerife South.

Is Playa de las Américas noisy?

Parts of it are, because it is the island's main nightlife area. Hotels away from the bar streets, or a base in neighbouring Costa Adeje or Los Cristianos, give quieter nights with the nightlife a short walk away.

Is Puerto de la Cruz worth staying in?

Yes, if you value a real town over guaranteed sunshine. It has a harbour, old streets, Playa Jardín and Loro Parque, with the Orotava Valley and Teide close by. Expect milder, cloudier weather than the south and a longer transfer from Tenerife South.

guides.title: Which Canary Island Is Best? All 8 Islands Compared
guides.summary: Compare all eight Canary Islands on beaches, weather and wind, nightlife, families, walking, quiet and flights from the UK and Ireland, then pick by trip type.
guides.html:
"The Canaries" is a weak answer to the question of where to go, because the eight islands of this Spanish archipelago are very different holidays. One is a volcano wrapped in resorts, another is a flat, windswept desert of beaches, a third is mostly cliffs and laurel forest with almost no sand. This guide compares all eight fairly, island by island, then answers the "best for" questions people actually ask. No single island wins on everything, and the right pick depends on what you will do all day.

A few things are the same everywhere. The Canary Islands are an autonomous community of Spain, they use the euro, they sit in the EU and Schengen area, they run one hour behind mainland Spain, and the emergency number is 112. Read entry requirements and local tips before you book.

The eight islands at a glance

IslandBest forBeachesWeather and windNightlifeGetting there from the UK and Ireland
TenerifeVariety, first visits, TeideGood, mostly in the south; many are dark sandSunny dry south, greener cloudier northPlenty, centred on Playa de las AméricasMany direct routes, two airports
Gran CanariaCity plus beach, mountain drivesLong golden beaches and dunes in the south, a city beach in Las PalmasSunny south, cooler cloudier northPlenty, in the south and in Las PalmasMany direct routes
LanzaroteVolcanic scenery, art, couplesSheltered coves in the south, surf beach in the northDry and often breezyModerate, mostly in Puerto del CarmenMany direct routes
FuerteventuraLong beaches, wind and water sportsLong stretches of pale sandDry and often windyLow key, livelier in CorralejoMany direct routes
La PalmaHiking, stargazingDark-sand beachesGreener, more cloud and rain on the east sideVery littleCheck current UK routes; connections via other islands
La GomeraWalking, quietDark-sand beaches and rocky covesMild, misty in the high forestVery littleFly to Tenerife, then ferry
El HierroDiving, real remotenessAlmost none; natural rock pools insteadMild, cloudier on the heightsAlmost noneConnect via Tenerife or Gran Canaria
La Graciosa (see Lanzarote)Walking and cyclingPale sand beaches reached on foot or by bikeDry and breezyNone to speak ofFly to Lanzarote, then a short ferry

Tenerife: the most varied island

Tenerife is the largest island and the one that does the most things reasonably well. The south, around Costa Adeje, Playa de las Américas and Los Cristianos, is dry, sunny and built for holidays: hotels, beaches such as Playa del Duque, water parks and most of the nightlife. The north, around Puerto de la Cruz and the Orotava Valley, is greener, cloudier and more Spanish in feel. Above everything sits Teide National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2007, with Spain's highest peak and a cable car.

The trade-off: the southern resorts are large and busy, and the best walking and old towns are a drive away. Tenerife has two airports, Tenerife South for the resorts and Tenerife North for the north. Our things to do in Tenerife and where to stay in Tenerife guides go deeper.

Gran Canaria: a real city and a long sunny south

Gran Canaria is the island to pick if you want a proper city as well as resorts. Las Palmas de Gran Canaria has the long urban beach of Las Canteras and the old quarter of Vegueta. In the south, Maspalomas, Playa del Inglés and Meloneras sit beside the Maspalomas dunes, and Puerto de Mogán is a quieter harbour village. The mountainous centre, with Roque Nublo, is the island's surprise: steep, pine-covered and excellent for walking and scenic driving.

The trade-off: the southern resort strip is dense, and the north of the island is often cloudy in winter. See things to do in Gran Canaria.

Lanzarote: volcanoes, design and calm

Lanzarote looks like nowhere else in Europe. Lava fields cover much of the south, and Timanfaya National Park protects the most dramatic of them. The artist César Manrique helped shape the island's approach to art and nature. Visitor sites include Jameos del Agua, Mirador del Río and the Jardín de Cactus. Vines grow in black volcanic hollows in La Geria.

Beaches split by coast: sheltered coves at Papagayo near Playa Blanca, a town beach at Puerto del Carmen, and wild surf at Famara. The trade-off: there is little shade and little green, and it is often breezy. More in things to do in Lanzarote.

Fuerteventura: beaches and wind

Fuerteventura is the beach island. Its coastline holds long stretches of pale sand: the Grandes Playas de Corralejo beside the Corralejo dunes, the lagoon of Sotavento in the south and the remote sweep of Cofete. The wind that shapes it makes it a centre for windsurfing and kitesurfing and surfing.

The trade-off: that same wind can sandblast a sunbathing day, the landscape inland is bare, and distances between sights are long. Corralejo is the liveliest base. See things to do in Fuerteventura.

La Palma: the walker's and stargazer's island

La Palma is steep, green and much quieter than the big four. The Caldera de Taburiente National Park and the ridge up to Roque de los Muchachos, home to an international observatory, give some of the best hiking and stargazing in the islands. Beaches include dark-sand bays, with Playa de Tazacorte a black-sand option on the west coast.

The trade-off: a car helps on the twisting roads. As of November 2026, Aena lists London Gatwick among the airport's destinations; check your own departure airport and dates. La Palma airport also has inter-island flights.

La Gomera: deep valleys and forest

La Gomera is small, round and cut by deep ravines. At its centre, Garajonay National Park protects laurel forest and has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1986. Walkers come for the trails and viewpoints such as the Mirador de Abrante; San Sebastián and Valle Gran Rey are possible bases.

The trade-off: dark-sand bays rather than long resort beaches, and quieter evenings, and no direct flights from the UK or Ireland. One option is to fly to Tenerife and take the ferry from Los Cristianos. La Gomera has a small inter-island airport too.

El Hierro: the far edge

El Hierro is a small island in the west of the archipelago and suits a quiet trip. It suits divers, walkers and anyone who wants to be genuinely away from it all. The marine reserve off La Restinga draws scuba divers; swimming is mostly in natural rock pools rather than on beaches.

The trade-off: getting there takes a connection (a ferry from Los Cristianos on Tenerife, or a flight to El Hierro's small inter-island airport), and there is little to do in the evening.

La Graciosa: no paved roads

La Graciosa, off the northern tip of Lanzarote and covered in our Lanzarote guide, is the smallest inhabited island. Its streets and tracks are sand, so people walk, cycle or take a 4x4 taxi to beaches such as Playa de las Conchas. Passenger ferries leave from Órzola on Lanzarote. It works best as a day trip or a night or two of real quiet.

Cost pressure, in words

Compare prices for your dates and type of stay. Include any car hire, ferries or connecting flights in your budget, and book accommodation before committing to transport. Winter is a popular time to seek sunshine; see the Canary Islands in winter and the best time to visit.

Best for: quick answers

  • First visit: Tenerife. It has the widest mix of beach, mountain, towns and day trips, plus direct flight options. Gran Canaria is a close second if you want a city.
  • Families: Tenerife's south for water parks and calm beaches, or Fuerteventura for wide sandy beaches, with swimming conditions checked locally. Gran Canaria's south works too.
  • Beaches: Fuerteventura, then Gran Canaria's dunes. Lanzarote's Papagayo coves are the pick for sheltered swimming. Our best beaches guide ranks them.
  • Hiking: La Palma and La Gomera, then Tenerife (Teide, Anaga, Masca) and central Gran Canaria.
  • Winter sun: the southern coasts of Tenerife and Gran Canaria, which are the most sheltered from the cloud the trade winds bring to the north. Lanzarote and Fuerteventura are dry but breezier. Check our weather page.
  • Couples: Lanzarote for design, food and wine, or La Gomera for walking and quiet.
  • No car: Gran Canaria (Las Palmas and the south are linked by frequent buses) or Tenerife (the southern resorts and the north are linked by buses, and Santa Cruz and La Laguna by tram). See getting around.

Combinations that work by ferry

Two islands in one trip is easy if you pick neighbours. Ferry times below are the operator's published crossing times as of November 2026; check the day's timetable before you plan around them.

  • Tenerife and La Gomera: the classic pair. Fred. Olsen lists the Los Cristianos to San Sebastián de La Gomera crossing at 50 minutes, short enough for a day trip, better as two or three nights.
  • Lanzarote and Fuerteventura: Playa Blanca to Corralejo is listed at 25 or 35 minutes, so the two islands combine easily, even as a day trip.
  • Lanzarote and La Graciosa: a short passenger crossing from Órzola.
  • Tenerife and Gran Canaria: Fred. Olsen lists Agaete to Santa Cruz de Tenerife at 80 minutes. Good for a city-plus-volcano trip.
  • Tenerife with La Palma or El Hierro: longer sailings from Los Cristianos (listed at 150 minutes to Santa Cruz de La Palma and 140 to Valverde). Many people fly instead.

Our island-hopping guide and the ferry and plane page cover routes and tickets, and the two-week island-hopping itinerary puts it together.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which Canary Island is best for a first visit?

Tenerife suits most first visits because it combines sunny southern beaches, Teide National Park, the green north and old towns such as La Laguna, with direct flight options. Gran Canaria is the alternative if you want a real city alongside the beach.

Which Canary Island has the best beaches?

Fuerteventura has long stretches of pale sand, including the beaches beside the Corralejo dunes and the Sotavento lagoon. Gran Canaria's Maspalomas dunes are a close rival, and Lanzarote's Papagayo coves offer sheltered swimming spots when conditions allow. Tenerife's beaches are good but many are dark sand.

Which Canary Island is the warmest in winter?

All eight are mild in winter. For sheltered sunshine, consider the southern coasts of Tenerife and Gran Canaria, which sit in the lee of the mountains. Lanzarote and Fuerteventura are dry but more often windy. Northern coasts and high ground see more cloud and rain.

Which Canary Island is the least windy?

Wind comes mainly from the trade winds, and the flatter eastern islands, Fuerteventura and Lanzarote, can feel exposed. The southern and western coasts of Tenerife and Gran Canaria can offer sheltered spots, although spots such as El Médano on Tenerife are windy and popular with kitesurfers.

Can I visit two Canary Islands in one trip?

Yes. Tenerife with La Gomera and Lanzarote with Fuerteventura are the easiest pairs, each linked by ferries of under an hour as of November 2026. Tenerife and Gran Canaria also connect by ferry, and inter-island flights link all the islands with airports.

Which Canary Island is best without a car?

Gran Canaria and Tenerife have the most useful public buses, and Tenerife also has a tram between Santa Cruz and La Laguna. A base in Las Palmas or in Tenerife's southern resorts works well without a car. On La Palma, La Gomera and El Hierro a car makes a big difference.

destinations.name: Corralejo
destinations.tagline: North Fuerteventura's beach town between the dunes, Lobos and the Lanzarote ferry
destinations.summary: Corralejo is north Fuerteventura's main resort: a harbour town beside the Corralejo dunes and their long beaches, with boats to Isla de Lobos and ferries to Lanzarote.
destinations.html:
Corralejo is a resort and fishing town on the northern tip of Fuerteventura, in the Canary Islands, in the municipality of La Oliva. It has kept a small harbour and an old quarter of narrow streets and seafood restaurants, with a long main street and newer hotels spreading south towards the dunes. Across the strait you can see the islet of Lobos and, beyond it, Lanzarote.

Just south of town begins Corralejo Dunes Natural Park, which the Cabildo of Fuerteventura gives as about 2,339 hectares of protected sand dunes and coast. Along its eastern edge lie the Grandes Playas de Corralejo, long beaches of pale sand and clear water, with the main road running between the dunes and the sea. Stay on the marked paths in the park: walking off them damages the dunes. A short way west, the volcano of Calderón Hondo has a trail to its crater rim.

What to do

  • Spend beach days at the Grandes Playas in the dunes park.
  • Take a boat to Isla de Lobos and walk its trails. The Cabildo field guide gives a crossing of about fifteen minutes; check your booked service's time as of November 2026. Visits are limited by a permit system run by the Cabildo, so check the current rules before you go.
  • Learn to surf or kitesurf with one of the town's schools.
  • Drive to El Cotillo for La Concha and its lagoons.
  • Walk up Calderón Hondo for views over the volcanic north.

Corralejo is a lively resort town in the north of Fuerteventura, with a choice of restaurants and evening bars, yet it stays far quieter than the big resorts of Tenerife or Gran Canaria. It suits couples, families and surfers who want a town base with beaches close by.

The harbour is the ferry link to Lanzarote: Fred. Olsen lists the crossing to Playa Blanca at 25 or 35 minutes as of November 2026, which makes a day trip to Lanzarote easy. Fuerteventura Airport (FUE) lies south, near Puerto del Rosario, and public bus journeys to Corralejo require a change in Puerto del Rosario. See the Fuerteventura 5-day itinerary for a plan.

destinations.name: Costa Adeje, Playa de las Américas and Los Cristianos
destinations.tagline: South Tenerife's main resort strip, from Playa del Duque to the Los Cristianos ferry port
destinations.summary: The resort coast of south-west Tenerife: Costa Adeje's hotels and Playa del Duque, lively Playa de las Américas and the port town of Los Cristianos, with ferries to La Gomera.
destinations.html:
Costa Adeje, Playa de las Américas and Los Cristianos form one continuous resort coast on the south-west of Tenerife, in the Canary Islands. It is a dry, sunny part of the island with a wide choice of places to stay. The strip runs along the shore of two municipalities, Adeje and Arona, and each section has its own character, from upmarket hotels in the north of Costa Adeje to the older working port of Los Cristianos at the southern end.

Costa Adeje, the northern part, has the newer hotels, a long seafront promenade and beaches such as Playa del Duque, a sandy bay with sunbeds and calm water on most days. Playa de las Américas, in the middle, is the busiest section, with bars, restaurants and the nightlife the south is known for, plus reef breaks used for surfing. Los Cristianos began as a fishing village and keeps a town feel around its harbour and sheltered beach; it is also the ferry port for La Gomera, a 50-minute Fred. Olsen crossing as of November 2026, and for sailings to La Palma and El Hierro.

What to do

  • Spend a beach day at Playa del Duque and walk the seafront promenade south.
  • Go to Siam Park, the water park in Costa Adeje.
  • Take a whale and dolphin trip; boats leave from the harbours along this coast.
  • See the Los Gigantes cliffs and drive on to the hamlet of Masca.
  • Drive up to Teide National Park and the Teide cable car for the day.
  • Take the ferry from Los Cristianos for a day on La Gomera and Garajonay National Park.

Beaches here vary in sand and exposure; check local flags before swimming. If you want wilder sand, El Médano lies east along the south coast. The resort strip suits families and couples who want sun, an easy promenade and plenty of restaurants within walking distance; groups looking for nightlife tend to stay around Playa de las Américas. Golf courses lie inland of the coast for those who play golf.

The strip is a short drive from Tenerife South Airport, and TITSA buses link it with the airport, Santa Cruz and other towns. It works well as a base for the whole south and west of Tenerife, while the greener north around Puerto de la Cruz is a day trip across or around the mountain. Compare areas in where to stay in Tenerife.

destinations.name: El Hierro
destinations.tagline: The most westerly Canary Island: a biosphere reserve and geopark known for diving
destinations.summary: El Hierro, the most westerly of the Canary Islands, is a quiet biosphere reserve and UNESCO geopark of volcanic cliffs, juniper woods and the Mar de las Calmas dive waters.
destinations.html:
El Hierro is the most westerly and one of the smallest of the Canary Islands, a quiet, rugged island of volcanic cones, cliffs and pine and juniper woods. The whole island was declared a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve in 2000 and is also a UNESCO Global Geopark, recognised for volcanic landscapes that include a submarine eruption off its south coast in 2011. Tourism is small-scale, and that is the point of coming.

The capital, Valverde, sits inland in the north-east, near the airport and the ferry port. To the north-west, the El Golfo valley is a vast amphitheatre of cliffs dropping to a fertile plain around Frontera, overlooked by the Mirador de la Peña, a viewpoint and restaurant designed by César Manrique. In the far west, the wind-twisted junipers of El Sabinar are one of the island's best-known sights. The south coast around La Restinga faces the Mar de las Calmas, a protected marine reserve with calm, clear water that draws divers.

What to do

  • Go scuba diving or snorkelling from La Restinga in the Mar de las Calmas.
  • Walk to El Sabinar and the far western tip of the island.
  • Look over the El Golfo valley from the Mirador de la Peña.
  • Hike the old paths across the island's high central ridge.
  • Swim in the natural rock pools along the coast, as there are few sandy beaches.

El Hierro suits divers, walkers and travellers who want to disconnect: there are no big resorts, little nightlife and few beaches. Compared with La Gomera it is wilder and further away; compared with La Palma it is smaller and lower. Weather on the coast is mild: AEMET's 1981 to 2010 normals for the El Hierro airport station give an average January high of 20.9C, an August high of 26.1C and 206 mm of rain a year, though the uplands are cooler and often cloudy.

The island has a small inter-island airport (VDE) near Valverde, with inter-island flights. By sea, Fred. Olsen lists a 140-minute crossing from Los Cristianos on Tenerife as of November 2026. A hire car is useful for exploring beyond the main towns. See island hopping by ferry and plane and the two-week island-hopping itinerary.

destinations.name: Fuerteventura
destinations.tagline: The long-beach island: dunes in the north, Jandía's sands in the south and steady wind
destinations.summary: Fuerteventura is the Canary Island of long beaches and wind: Corralejo's dunes in the north, Sotavento and Cofete on the Jandía peninsula, and a quiet, dry interior.
destinations.html:
Fuerteventura is the second-largest of the Canary Islands and the closest to the African coast, a long, dry island of open plains, eroded volcanic hills and beaches. It is best known for the length and number of its sandy beaches and for the steady trade winds that make it a centre for windsurfing and kitesurfing. The whole island, with a band of sea around it, has been a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve since May 2009.

Think of the island in three parts. The north has the resort town of Corralejo, the dunes of Corralejo Dunes Natural Park with the Grandes Playas, and the fishing village of El Cotillo with its La Concha beach and lagoons. The centre holds the capital, Puerto del Rosario, near Fuerteventura Airport (FUE), the old inland capital of Betancuria and the sea caves of Ajuy. The south is the Jandía peninsula, with the lagoon beach of Sotavento on the east side and the remote Playa de Cofete on the west, reached by an unpaved road.

The climate is dry: AEMET's 1981 to 2010 normals for the Fuerteventura airport station give 98 mm of rain a year, an average January high of 20.6C and an August high of 27.8C. Wind is the factor to plan around: great for sailors and surfers, less so for sunbathers on exposed beaches.

What to do

  • Walk the dunes and swim at the Grandes Playas de Corralejo.
  • Learn to kite or windsurf at Sotavento, or catch the Fuerteventura Kite Festival.
  • Climb the crater of Calderón Hondo in the north.
  • Visit Betancuria and the coastal caves at Ajuy.
  • Try queso majorero, the island's goat's cheese.
  • Go surfing on the north coast reefs.

Fuerteventura suits beach lovers, water-sports fans and travellers who want space and quiet over sightseeing. It has less to visit than Lanzarote, its neighbour across a short ferry crossing, and lower hills and less tree cover than Tenerife or Gran Canaria, with long stretches of open beach. Plan with things to do in Fuerteventura and the Fuerteventura 5-day itinerary.

destinations.name: Gran Canaria
destinations.tagline: Round island of dunes in the south, a capital city in the north and peaks in between
destinations.summary: Gran Canaria pairs the Maspalomas dunes and southern resorts with Las Palmas, a real city on a city beach, and a mountainous interior of UNESCO-listed sacred sites.
destinations.html:
Gran Canaria is the third-largest of the Canary Islands, a near-round island with the mountains in the middle and the coast all around. Its capital, Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, is a major city in the archipelago and shares the role of regional capital with Santa Cruz de Tenerife. The south has extensive holiday accommodation, around Maspalomas, Playa del Inglés and Meloneras, where the weather is generally dry.

The island divides into three zones. The north and north-east hold the capital, the port and the greener farmland around towns such as Agaete, where the Bajada de la Rama festival takes place each August. The south is the resort coast, from the Maspalomas Dunes west to Puerto de Mogán and coves such as Playa de Amadores. The interior climbs to rock pinnacles like Roque Nublo and the cultural landscape of Risco Caído and the Sacred Mountains, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since July 2019. Almost half of the island has been a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve since 2005.

AEMET's 1981 to 2010 normals for the Gran Canaria airport station, on the east coast, give an average January high of 20.8C, an August high of 27.5C and 151 mm of rain a year. The north of the island is cloudier and the high interior is noticeably cooler, so bring a layer for the mountains even in summer.

What to do

  • Walk the Maspalomas Dunes to Playa de Maspalomas.
  • Explore Vegueta, the old quarter of Las Palmas, and swim at Playa de las Canteras.
  • Hike to Roque Nublo in the centre of the island.
  • Spend an evening in the harbour of Puerto de Mogán.
  • Make the long walk to the remote west-coast beach of Güigüí.
  • Join the Las Palmas de Gran Canaria Carnival or watch the Transgrancanaria trail race.

Gran Canaria suits travellers who want a beach holiday with a city close by: Las Palmas offers a substantial urban base. Compared with Tenerife the mountains are lower but the interior is just as dramatic, and the southern dunes offer a different coastal landscape. Fuerteventura and Lanzarote are flatter and windier. Flights land at Gran Canaria Airport (LPA), between the capital and the south, and Fred. Olsen lists the Agaete to Santa Cruz de Tenerife ferry at 80 minutes as of November 2026.

Plan with things to do in Gran Canaria and the Gran Canaria 7-day itinerary.

destinations.name: La Gomera
destinations.tagline: Ravines, terraced valleys and the laurel forest of Garajonay, 50 minutes from Tenerife
destinations.summary: La Gomera is a small, steep island of deep ravines and terraced valleys around the UNESCO-listed laurel forest of Garajonay, home of the Silbo Gomero whistled language.
destinations.html:
La Gomera is one of the smaller Canary Islands, a round, high island west of Tenerife cut by deep ravines that run from the central plateau to the sea. At its centre lies Garajonay National Park, which covers 3,984 hectares, about a tenth of the island, and has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1986 for its laurel forest, a type of humid forest that has almost vanished elsewhere. The highest point, Alto de Garajonay, reaches 1,487 metres.

The island has no large resorts. The capital, San Sebastián de La Gomera, is the ferry port on the east coast. Valle Gran Rey, in the west, is a valley of palm groves and terraces that ends at a small beach town popular with long-stay visitors. In the north, the green valleys around Hermigua and Agulo face Tenerife and Mount Teide across the sea, and the glass-floored Mirador de Abrante hangs over the cliffs above Agulo. La Gomera is also home to the Silbo Gomero, a whistled form of Spanish used to talk across ravines, recognised by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage in 2009 and still taught in island schools.

What to do

  • Hike the misty trails of Garajonay National Park.
  • Stand on the glass platform of the Mirador de Abrante.
  • Drive the winding road down into Valle Gran Rey for the sunset.
  • Try almogrote, the island's spicy cheese spread, and local palm honey.
  • Look for pilot whales and dolphins on a whale and dolphin trip in the channel between La Gomera and Tenerife.

La Gomera suits walkers and travellers who want quiet, landscape and small hotels or rural houses over beaches; most beaches are pebble or black sand. It is accessible by a short ferry crossing from Tenerife: Fred. Olsen lists the Los Cristianos to San Sebastián crossing at 50 minutes as of November 2026, so many people visit on a day trip from Costa Adeje in the south of Tenerife. That is enough to drive through Garajonay, but the island repays a few nights.

La Gomera also has a small airport (GMZ) in the south with inter-island flights. Compared with La Palma and El Hierro it is close to Tenerife. Combine the three in the two-week island-hopping itinerary.
destinations.region: La Palma, La Gomera and El Hierro

destinations.name: La Palma
destinations.tagline: Steep, green island of the Caldera de Taburiente, dark skies and recent volcanoes
destinations.summary: La Palma is the Canary Islands' hiking and stargazing island: the Caldera de Taburiente, observatories on Roque de los Muchachos and the new lava of the 2021 eruption.
destinations.html:
La Palma is the north-westernmost of the Canary Islands, a steep, green island often called La Isla Bonita. It rises to 2,426 metres at the Roque de los Muchachos, on the rim of the huge erosion crater protected as Caldera de Taburiente National Park. The Roque de los Muchachos Observatory, run by the Instituto de Astrofísica de Canarias, sits near the summit at 2,396 metres, and the island's dark night skies draw stargazers as well as astronomers.

The island is narrow and mountainous, so most roads are winding. The capital, Santa Cruz de La Palma, on the east coast, is a small port town of balconied houses and the home of the Los Indianos carnival party. La Palma Airport (SPC) lies just south of it. The west side, around Los Llanos de Aridane and Tazacorte, is sunnier, with banana plantations and the black-sand Playa de Tazacorte. The south is a ridge of young volcanoes.

That volcanic story is recent. The Tajogaite eruption on the west side began on 19 September 2021 and lasted 85 days and 8 hours, ending on 13 December 2021. Some of the area can be visited on guided routes; see volcano and lava tube visits and follow current local rules for access.

What to do

  • Drive or hike to Roque de los Muchachos for views into the caldera and above the clouds.
  • Hike into the Caldera de Taburiente or along the volcano ridge in the south.
  • Spend a night stargazing from one of the island's viewpoints.
  • Join the white-clad crowds at Los Indianos on Carnival Monday in Santa Cruz.
  • Swim at Playa de Tazacorte and try local wines.

La Palma suits walkers, stargazers and travellers who want a quiet, green island with few large resorts. It is not a beach island: the coast is mostly rocky, with a few black-sand beaches. Compared with its western neighbours La Gomera and El Hierro it is larger and higher, with more choice of places to stay. Besides flights, Fred. Olsen lists a 150-minute crossing from Los Cristianos on Tenerife to Santa Cruz de La Palma as of November 2026. See the island-hopping guide.
destinations.region: La Palma, La Gomera and El Hierro

destinations.name: Lanzarote
destinations.tagline: Volcanic island shaped by César Manrique, with La Graciosa off its northern tip
destinations.summary: Lanzarote is the volcanic island of Timanfaya's lava fields, La Geria's walled vines and César Manrique's art, with resort beaches in the south and La Graciosa a short ferry away.
destinations.html:
Lanzarote is the easternmost of the Canary Islands, a low, dry and strikingly volcanic island off the coast of Africa. Eruptions between 1730 and 1736 buried a large part of its south-west under lava, now protected as Timanfaya National Park. The whole island has been a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve since 1993. What sets Lanzarote apart is how it looks: low white houses, black lava and green doors and windows, a style the artist César Manrique championed and that still governs much of the island's building.

The island is compact and easy to drive. The resorts are on the south and east coast: Puerto del Carmen, a major resort, close to Lanzarote Airport (ACE), and Playa Blanca at the southern tip, near the Papagayo beaches. The capital, Arrecife, sits between the airport and the north. The north holds most of the Manrique sites: Jameos del Agua, the Cueva de los Verdes, the Mirador del Río and the Jardín de Cactus. The west coast has the surf beach of Famara and the green lagoon at El Golfo.

Off the northern tip lies La Graciosa, the eighth inhabited Canary Island, reached by frequent ferries from Órzola. It has sand tracks instead of tarmac roads and beaches such as Playa de las Conchas. AEMET's 1981 to 2010 normals for the Lanzarote airport station give an average January high of 20.7C, an August high of 29.1C and 111 mm of rain a year, so expect dry weather and frequent trade winds.

What to do

  • Tour the lava fields of Timanfaya and the vineyards of La Geria, with a stop for wine tasting.
  • Visit the César Manrique Foundation in his former home, built into lava bubbles.
  • Explore lava tubes at Cueva de los Verdes and Jameos del Agua.
  • Swim at Papagayo or Caletón Blanco, and surf at Famara.
  • Take the ferry to La Graciosa for a day on its beaches.
  • Watch or race in Ironman Lanzarote, or cycle the island's quiet roads.

Lanzarote suits couples and families who want reliable sun, art and landscape over nightlife, and cyclists and triathletes who train on its roads. Compared with Tenerife and Gran Canaria it is flatter, drier and more uniform in style; compared with Fuerteventura it has fewer long beaches but far more sights. Fred. Olsen lists the Playa Blanca to Corralejo crossing at 25 or 35 minutes as of November 2026. Plan with things to do in Lanzarote and the Lanzarote 5-day itinerary.

destinations.name: Las Palmas de Gran Canaria
destinations.tagline: Gran Canaria's capital: a city beach, the old quarter of Vegueta and a big carnival
destinations.summary: Las Palmas, the capital of Gran Canaria and a major city in the Canary Islands, combines a city beach at Las Canteras with the old quarter of Vegueta and a year-round local life.
destinations.html:
Las Palmas de Gran Canaria is the capital of Gran Canaria and a major city in the Canary Islands, set on the north-east corner of the island around a large commercial port. Together with Santa Cruz de Tenerife it is one of the two capitals of the archipelago. It is a working city rather than a resort, which is much of its appeal: you share the beach, the markets and the bars with the people who live here, in a climate that stays mild all year.

The city stretches along a narrow strip between two coasts. On the west side, Playa de las Canteras runs for several kilometres in front of a seafront promenade, sheltered by a natural rock reef offshore that calms the water at its central section and makes it good for snorkelling. To the south lies Vegueta, the old quarter where the city was founded, with the cathedral of Santa Ana and the Casa de Colón, a museum exploring the island's connections with Columbus and the Americas. Next to it, Triana is the historic shopping street area.

What to do

  • Walk the promenade and swim at Playa de las Canteras.
  • Explore the lanes of Vegueta and the Casa de Colón.
  • Join the Las Palmas de Gran Canaria Carnival, one of the islands' biggest street festivals.
  • Try Canarian food in the city markets: papas arrugadas with mojo, ropa vieja and gofio.
  • Take a day trip into the mountains to Roque Nublo.
  • Surf at La Cícer on Las Canteras, a city break with surfing on the doorstep.

The city suits travellers who want culture, food and a real place to live in for a week or a month, with a beach on the doorstep; it is popular with long-stay winter visitors and remote workers for that reason. The north of the island is cloudier than the south, so if your priority is guaranteed sun, the southern resorts of Maspalomas are the better base. The two are linked by fast Global buses along the motorway.

Gran Canaria Airport (LPA) lies south of the city on the east coast. From the city you can reach the whole island by bus or car: see the Gran Canaria guide and the Gran Canaria 7-day itinerary.

destinations.name: Maspalomas, Playa del Inglés and Meloneras
destinations.tagline: South Gran Canaria's resort coast, framed by the Maspalomas dunes
destinations.summary: Maspalomas, Playa del Inglés and Meloneras form south Gran Canaria's resort coast: protected sand dunes, long beaches, the lighthouse promenade and the island's driest weather.
destinations.html:
Maspalomas is the main resort area of Gran Canaria, in the Canary Islands, spread along the island's southern tip in the municipality of San Bartolomé de Tirajana. It takes in three linked areas: Playa del Inglés to the east, the dunes and lagoon of Maspalomas in the middle, and Meloneras to the west. This is a dry, sunny part of Gran Canaria with extensive resort accommodation.

The centrepiece is the Maspalomas Dunes, a protected field of sand dunes between the two resorts, with a small lagoon, La Charca, at its western edge. The dunes meet the sea along Playa de Maspalomas, which continues east into Playa del Inglés, together one long sweep of sand. The Maspalomas lighthouse marks the western end, where a promenade leads on to Meloneras and its newer hotels. Stay on the marked paths through the dunes: the protected area has rules on where you can walk.

What to do

  • Walk across the Maspalomas Dunes early in the morning, before the sand heats up.
  • Spend a beach day on Playa del Inglés or Playa de Maspalomas.
  • Stroll the lighthouse promenade from Maspalomas to Meloneras at sunset.
  • Drive west to the harbour of Puerto de Mogán and the calm cove of Playa de Amadores.
  • Head inland to Roque Nublo for a mountain day, or play a round of golf near the resort.

Playa del Inglés is the busiest section, with apartments, shopping centres and a well-known LGBTQ+ scene. Maspalomas and Meloneras are quieter, with more hotels and resort complexes. The area suits families, couples and winter-sun visitors looking for reliable weather and a long beach; it has less local town life than Las Palmas, which is linked by bus and road.

Gran Canaria Airport (LPA) lies up the east coast, a straightforward motorway transfer. From Maspalomas the rest of the island is easy to reach, from the mountain interior to the western coast and the remote beach of Güigüí. See things to do in Gran Canaria for more ideas.

destinations.name: Playa Blanca
destinations.tagline: Lanzarote's southern tip: a quieter resort near the Papagayo beaches and the Fuerteventura ferry
destinations.summary: Playa Blanca is the quiet resort at Lanzarote's southern tip: a seafront path to Marina Rubicón, the Papagayo coves nearby and ferries across to Corralejo on Fuerteventura.
destinations.html:
Playa Blanca is a resort town at the southern tip of Lanzarote, in the Canary Islands, in the municipality of Yaiza. It started as a small fishing settlement and has grown into a spread-out resort of low-rise hotels, villas and apartments, quieter and more relaxed than Puerto del Carmen. On clear days you can see Fuerteventura and the islet of Lobos across the strait.

A seafront path runs for several kilometres along the coast, linking the town beach, the ferry port and the Marina Rubicón, a yacht harbour lined with restaurants. East of town, the Papagayo beaches are a series of sandy coves set in the protected landscape of Los Ajaches, reached on foot along the coast or by an unpaved track. The water there is clear and usually calm, and the coves are the main reason many visitors choose Playa Blanca.

What to do

  • Swim and snorkel at the Papagayo coves.
  • Walk the seafront path to Marina Rubicón for dinner by the water.
  • Drive up the west coast to the green lagoon at El Golfo and the salt pans of Janubio.
  • Tour Timanfaya National Park, a short drive north.
  • Take the ferry to Corralejo for a day on Fuerteventura's dunes and beaches.

The ferry is one of Playa Blanca's practical strengths: Fred. Olsen lists the crossing to Corralejo at 25 or 35 minutes as of November 2026, and Baleària Canarias also sails the same route. That makes two-island trips easy; see island hopping by ferry and plane and the island-hopping guide.

Playa Blanca suits couples and families who want calm evenings, good swimming and easy access to the south-west of Lanzarote, rather than nightlife. It is further from Lanzarote Airport (ACE) than the eastern resorts, but the transfer follows the main roads through the south of the island. A hire car makes the most of the area, since the Papagayo track and the west coast are poorly served by buses.
