destinations.name: Puerto de la Cruz and the Orotava Valley
destinations.tagline: North Tenerife's long-established resort town, below the green Orotava Valley and Mount Teide
destinations.summary: Puerto de la Cruz is north Tenerife's long-established resort town: Manrique's Lago Martiánez pools, black-sand Playa Jardín, Loro Parque and the green Orotava Valley above.
destinations.html:
Puerto de la Cruz sits on the north coast of Tenerife, in the Canary Islands, at the foot of the Orotava Valley, a broad green slope of farms and villages climbing towards Mount Teide. It is a long-established resort town with a Spanish town centre of squares, churches and a small fishing harbour, and a gentler pace than the southern resorts. The weather is milder and cloudier than in the south, and the reward is a greener landscape and everyday town life.

The town's best-known sight is Lago Martiánez, a complex of seawater pools and terraces designed by the Lanzarote artist César Manrique. West of the centre, Playa Jardín is a black-sand beach laid out with gardens behind it. The Atlantic on this coast is rougher than in the south, so check the flags before swimming. On the edge of town, Loro Parque is the zoo and marine park many families come for.

What to do

  • Swim in the Lago Martiánez seawater pools, then walk the seafront to the old harbour.
  • Spend an afternoon at Playa Jardín and its gardens.
  • Visit Loro Parque on the edge of town.
  • Walk the old streets and manor houses of La Orotava, up the valley, and see the Corpus Christi flower and sand carpets if you are there for the festival.
  • Drive west to the Drago Milenario in Icod de los Vinos.
  • Go up to Teide National Park; the road from the Orotava Valley is one of the main routes to the crater.

Puerto de la Cruz is a good base for hiking in the north and for touring the island without the resort crowds. The UNESCO-listed old town of La Laguna, the capital Santa Cruz and the forest of Anaga Rural Park are all within an easy drive to the east. Hotels range from long-established town hotels to apartments, and many visitors return year after year for the climate and the town life.

The nearest airport is Tenerife North (TFN), above La Laguna; Tenerife South (TFS) is further away on the far side of the island. To compare the town with the southern resorts of Costa Adeje, read where to stay in Tenerife, or see the whole island in the Tenerife guide.

destinations.name: Puerto del Carmen
destinations.tagline: Lanzarote's main tourist resort: a long beach promenade and an old fishing harbour
destinations.summary: Puerto del Carmen is Lanzarote's main tourist resort: Playa Grande and a long seafront avenue of restaurants and bars, a quieter old harbour for diving, and the airport close by.
destinations.html:
Puerto del Carmen is a major holiday resort on Lanzarote, in the Canary Islands, on the island's south-east coast in the municipality of Tías. It grew from a small fishing village into a resort that stretches for several kilometres along a seafront avenue, the Avenida de las Playas, lined with restaurants, bars and shops on one side and beaches on the other. Despite its size it keeps Lanzarote's low-rise, white-walled look.

The main beach, Playa Grande, is a broad sweep of golden sand that Turismo Lanzarote gives as 1,190 metres long, with lifeguards, sunbeds and a promenade. It forms part of a run of beaches along this coast that continues east to Los Pocillos and Matagorda. At the western end, the old town and harbour are quieter: fishing boats, seafood restaurants and the small beach where many of the island's scuba diving schools start their shore dives.

What to do

  • Spend beach days on Playa Grande and walk the seafront avenue.
  • Try scuba diving or snorkelling from the old harbour.
  • Drive west to Timanfaya National Park and the vineyards of La Geria, both close by.
  • Visit the César Manrique Foundation and the northern sights such as Jameos del Agua.
  • Eat Canarian dishes like papas arrugadas with mojo in the old town.

Puerto del Carmen suits families and couples who want a full-service resort with plenty of choice for eating out, plus groups looking for evening bars along the strip. It is busier than Playa Blanca, and its beaches are more urban than the coves at Papagayo. Its central position means no part of Lanzarote is a long drive away.

Lanzarote Airport (ACE) is just up the coast, a convenient airport transfer. Buses run along the coast to the airport and the capital, Arrecife, though a hire car is the easiest way to see the island. For a full plan, see things to do in Lanzarote and the Lanzarote 5-day itinerary.

destinations.name: Tenerife
destinations.tagline: The largest Canary Island: Mount Teide, sunny south resorts and a green north
destinations.summary: Tenerife, the largest of the Canary Islands, splits into a dry, sunny resort south and a greener north of old towns, with Mount Teide, the highest peak in Spain, in between.
destinations.html:
Tenerife is the largest of the Canary Islands, a Spanish island in the Atlantic off north-west Africa, and a popular choice for first-time visitors. Its layout is shaped by Mount Teide, which rises to 3,715 metres, the highest peak in Spain, at the centre of Teide National Park. The park has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2007. The mountain divides the island into two halves with different weather and a different feel, and picking a side is the first decision of any trip.

The south and south-west are dry, sunny and built around holidays. The resort strip of Costa Adeje, Playa de las Américas and Los Cristianos lies close to Tenerife South Airport and offers hotels, beaches such as Playa del Duque and the Siam Park water park. Further east, El Médano is the island's wind and kite beach. The north is greener and cloudier, with more of everyday Canarian life: Puerto de la Cruz and the Orotava Valley, the old university town of San Cristóbal de La Laguna (a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1999) and the capital, Santa Cruz de Tenerife, home of the Auditorio de Tenerife and the Santa Cruz de Tenerife Carnival.

The weather gap is real. AEMET's 1981 to 2010 normals for the Tenerife Sur airport station give 132 mm of rain a year and an average January high of 21.7C. The Tenerife Norte airport station, on the upland plain of Los Rodeos near La Laguna, records 520 mm and a January high of 16.0C. The north coast at Puerto de la Cruz is milder than that upland station, but the northern side is often cloudier.

What to do

  • Ride the Teide cable car, or plan a summit climb with the Teide permit and cable car guide.
  • Drive the mountain road to the hamlet of Masca, then see the Los Gigantes cliffs from the sea.
  • Walk the laurel forest trails of Anaga Rural Park and swim at Playa de las Teresitas or the black sand of Playa de Benijo.
  • Visit the ancient dragon tree, the Drago Milenario in Icod de los Vinos.
  • Book a whale and dolphin trip from the south-west coast, or go stargazing in the national park.

Tenerife suits first-time visitors, families after dependable sun in the south, and walkers who want mountain and forest trails. Compared with Gran Canaria it has the higher mountain. Compared with Lanzarote and Fuerteventura it is greener and more varied, with fewer long natural sandy beaches. It has two airports, Tenerife South (TFS) for the resorts and Tenerife North (TFN) near La Laguna, and it is the main ferry base for the western islands: Fred. Olsen lists the Los Cristianos to La Gomera crossing at 50 minutes as of November 2026, with sailings from Los Cristianos to La Palma and El Hierro too.

For planning, start with things to do in Tenerife, where to stay in Tenerife and the Tenerife 7-day itinerary. If you are still choosing an island, read which Canary Island is best.

beaches.name: Caletón Blanco
beaches.tagline: White sand and calm pools among black lava near Órzola, north Lanzarote
beaches.summary: A small white-sand beach set in black lava near Órzola in the far north of Lanzarote. Calm, clear water for swimming and snorkelling, and a car park.
beaches.html:
Caletón Blanco is a patch of white sand set among the black lava of the north-east coast of Lanzarote, just south of the fishing port of Órzola in the municipality of Haría. The contrast between pale sand, dark rock and clear, shallow water is what draws people here, and the tourism board rates its occupancy as high, so expect company.

The lava breaks the coast into small inlets, creating sheltered pools, and both the island tourism board and Spain's national tourism site describe the bathing conditions as calm. Spain's tourism site calls it excellent for scuba diving and snorkelling. There is a car park beside the coast road, but no other services are listed: lifeguards, kiosks and sunbeds are not confirmed by these listings, so bring your own supplies and shade.

Before you go

  • Car park next to the LZ-1 coast road; Turismo Lanzarote lists a bus service to the area.
  • No lifeguard service or facilities are listed. Bring water, food and shade.
  • Wear water shoes: the inlets are edged with sharp volcanic rock.
  • Arrive early on weekends and in summer, when the small beach fills up.

Caletón Blanco fits easily into a day in the north of the island, with Jameos del Agua, Cueva de los Verdes and the Mirador del Río all close by. Ferries for La Graciosa leave from Órzola, so you can pair it with a trip to Playa de las Conchas. See our snorkelling guide for other calm-water spots.

beaches.name: Grandes Playas de Corralejo
beaches.tagline: Three and a half kilometres of white sand below the Corralejo dunes
beaches.summary: A 3.4 km run of white sand south of Corralejo on Fuerteventura, backed by the dunes of the natural park. Gentle to moderate waves and a Blue Flag in 2026.
beaches.html:
The Grandes Playas are the long beaches that run south-east from Corralejo, on the north coast of Fuerteventura, in the municipality of La Oliva. The La Oliva council measures them at 3,450 metres long and around 60 metres wide, from the Tres Islas hotel to the Barreta de Abajo beach, and the stretch takes in several named beaches: Playa de los Matos, Playa Larga, Playa del Viejo, Playa del Pozo and Playa del Caserón. Behind them rise the white dunes of the Corralejo Dunes Natural Park, and across the water you look over to the island of Lobos and the south of Lanzarote.

The sand is white and fairly coarse, and the council describes the waves as gentle to moderate. Conditions change with the wind, which is often strong on this coast: on calm days the water is good for swimming, on windy days it suits kitesurfers and windsurfers more than families. The Grandes Playas are on the 2026 Blue Flag list published by ADEAC. Because the beach is so long, you can nearly always find a quiet patch by walking away from the access points.

Things to know

  • Blue Flag beach in 2026. Check the flag and any posted information at the stretch where you settle.
  • The coast road south from Corralejo crosses the natural park and gives access along the beach.
  • The dunes are protected: stay on marked paths and do not take sand.
  • Services vary by section: lifeguards, sunbeds and parasols are listed at El Caserón. Bring supplies for unserviced stretches.

Corralejo is also the port for boats to Lobos and ferries to Lanzarote, which makes this a good base for island hopping. On the other side of the island's north, the beaches of El Cotillo offer reef-sheltered coves; check conditions on the day. Plan the rest of your stay with our things to do in Fuerteventura guide and the Fuerteventura 5-day itinerary.

beaches.name: Playa de Amadores
beaches.tagline: Sheltered white-sand bay in Mogán, south-west Gran Canaria
beaches.summary: A sheltered 488-metre bay of white sand in Mogán, south-west Gran Canaria, with calm water, a lifeguard service, sun loungers and restaurants along the back.
beaches.html:
Playa de Amadores lies on the south-west coast of Gran Canaria, in the municipality of Mogán, just west of Puerto Rico. It is a curved bay of white sand about 488 metres long and 50 metres wide, with a promenade of shops, bars and restaurants running behind the sand. The Mogán council's tourism site describes the bathing conditions simply as calm water, and that is the reason most people come.

The beach is fully set up for a lazy day: the council lists toilets, foot showers, a lifeguard, sun loungers and parasols for hire, and water-sports rental. The council rates occupancy as medium; this is not a guarantee of space on the day you visit. The generally calm water makes Amadores a family option, but check bathing flags rather than assuming that conditions elsewhere predict safety here.

Visiting Amadores

  • White sand and generally calm water; check bathing flags before swimming.
  • Lifeguard service, toilets, foot showers and sun loungers and parasols for hire.
  • Water-sports rental on the beach.
  • Bars, restaurants and shops along the promenade behind the sand.

Amadores is a short drive from the fishing harbour and canals of Puerto de Mogán to the west, and from the dunes and long beaches of Maspalomas to the east, including Playa de Maspalomas. The wild beach of Güigüí, much further up the west coast, is the opposite experience.

beaches.name: Playa de Benijo
beaches.tagline: Wild black-sand beach below the Anaga sea stacks
beaches.summary: A wild 300-metre black-sand beach on Tenerife's Anaga coast. Council notices warn of closed access because of rockfall risk: check before planning a visit.
beaches.html:
Playa de Benijo lies at the far north-eastern tip of Tenerife, past the villages of Taganana and Almáciga on the Anaga coast. It is about 300 metres of black sand at the foot of steep green slopes, with the Roques de Anaga, a group of sea stacks, rising out of the water offshore. Nothing has been built on the beach, and the official Tenerife tourism site lists only bins and a cleaning service.

The usual access is a path with steps, with no step-free route. The council has published an access-closure notice because of rockfall risk. Do not use a closed path or try alternative routes; check the latest council notice before travelling. This is open north coast, and the island's tourism site warns that the waves here are usually strong. Do not plan a beach walk or swim while access is closed. The beach is also popular with naturists. A few restaurants near the road at the top serve local food.

Visiting Benijo

  • Council notice: access closed because of rockfall risk. Check the latest notice before travelling.
  • Strong Atlantic waves: swimming is often unsafe.
  • No sunbeds, toilets or showers; restaurants are up by the road.
  • Limited parking, with fewer than 50 spaces.

The drive to Benijo crosses the laurel forest of Anaga Rural Park, one of the best areas on the island for hiking. For a beach alternative, choose the sheltered Playa de las Teresitas on the way back to Santa Cruz, or with the old streets of La Laguna.

beaches.name: Playa de Cofete
beaches.tagline: Fuerteventura's wild west-coast beach under the Jandía mountains
beaches.summary: A vast, empty beach on the windward side of the Jandía peninsula in south Fuerteventura, reached by unpaved track. Spectacular, but rough sea and no lifeguard surveillance.
beaches.html:
Playa de Cofete stretches along the windward, west-facing coast of the Jandía peninsula, at the southern end of Fuerteventura in the municipality of Pájara. Behind it, the mountains of Jandía rise in a great curved wall that the Pájara council describes as one of the most spectacular views in the Canary Islands. The whole area lies inside the Parque Natural de Jandía. The Pájara council measures Cofete itself at 6,000 metres; Spain's national tourism site uses a broader measurement of 13.7 kilometres. These listings describe different extents.

There are no resorts here, only the small hamlet of Cofete and its old cemetery near the shore. The sand is golden, and Spain's tourism site lists nudism as allowed and notes that sea turtles are released on this beach. The bathing conditions are another matter: the official listing describes them as windy with strong waves, and this exposed Atlantic coast is a place for walking and looking rather than swimming.

Getting there and staying safe

  • The route from Morro Jable leaves the paved road and continues as an unpaved track over the mountains to Cofete; the Cabildo de Fuerteventura resurfaced it in December 2025 after storm damage.
  • Public bus line 111 (Morro Jable, Cofete, Punta de Jandía) also serves the track; check the current timetable with the operator, Tiadhe.
  • The island tourism page marks the beach as unguarded and lists parking and a restaurant in the hamlet. Bring water, food, sun protection and a windproof layer.
  • Do not swim. Stay out of the water and keep back from the breaking waves.

Pair Cofete with the calmer Playa de Sotavento on the other side of the peninsula. The dark, remote skies of southern Fuerteventura also make this a good corner for stargazing, and the Fuerteventura 5-day itinerary shows how to fit the south of the island into a short trip.

beaches.name: Playa de El Médano
beaches.tagline: South Tenerife's windsurf beach below Montaña Roja
beaches.summary: A 750-metre grey-sand beach at El Médano, south Tenerife: calmer water by the town, wind and a water-sports area further along, below Montaña Roja.
beaches.html:
Playa de El Médano runs along the edge of the town of El Médano, in the municipality of Granadilla de Abona on the south coast of Tenerife. It is a long beach of fine grey sand, around 750 metres in length, with views of Montaña Roja, a red volcanic cone standing on its own by the sea. The official Tenerife tourism site calls El Médano the island's main hub for wind sports, and the steady breeze that blows down this coast is what gives the town its character.

The beach changes as you walk along it. The section closest to the town has the smallest waves and suits families, with toilets, showers, bars and sun loungers for hire. Further along, towards Montaña Roja, the water is rougher and the wind stronger: this is where windsurfers and kitesurfers launch, and it is the busiest stretch on a windy afternoon. A seafront promenade lined with surf shops, cafés and restaurants follows the sand. The wind that suits sailors can also make sunbathing gritty, so a windbreak helps on breezy days.

What to expect

  • Fine grey sand, with views of the Montaña Roja volcanic cone.
  • Gentler water near the town; wind and waves increase towards the cone.
  • Toilets, showers, bars, restaurants and sun loungers and parasols for hire.
  • A designated windsurfing area, with surf shops along the promenade. The council lists a lifeguard service.

El Médano is close to Tenerife South Airport, which makes it a handy first or last stop on a trip. If you want to learn, see our guide to windsurfing and kitesurfing in the Canary Islands. For another resort beach head west to Playa del Duque in Costa Adeje, and for a day inland, Teide National Park is a drive up the mountain.

facts.value: Large parking areas near the beach; inter-city buses stop in town

beaches.name: Playa de Famara
beaches.tagline: Lanzarote surf beach under the Famara cliffs, with strong currents
beaches.summary: Several kilometres of golden sand under the Famara cliffs on Lanzarote's north-west coast. A surf beach with big waves, wind and strong currents.
beaches.html:
Playa de Famara runs for several kilometres along the north-west coast of Lanzarote, in the municipality of Teguise. It starts at the small village of La Caleta de Famara and follows the shore to the foot of the Risco de Famara, the long cliff wall that closes the view to the north. The sand is fine and golden-brown, and the trade winds have piled it into low dunes with sparse plants at the back of the beach.

Famara is a surf beach rather than a swimming beach. There are usually waves and wind, which is why surf schools, kitesurfers and windfoilers use it, and paragliders and hang gliders often launch from the top of the cliff. The beach changes a lot with the tide: at low water the sea pulls back and leaves wide, shallow pools and a sheet of wet sand that mirrors the cliffs; at high tide parts of the beach disappear and the waves reach the rounded volcanic boulders along the top.

Bathing safety

  • The Teguise tourism office warns: "exercise extreme caution when swimming, as this is a beach with strong waves and powerful ocean currents".
  • Turismo Lanzarote lists danger signage and a lifeguard service among the beach services; swim only where and when lifeguards are on duty, and follow the flags.
  • Fires and barbecues are prohibited on the beach.
  • Learning to surf here is best done with a school, which will pick the right spot for the tide.

Read our guides to surfing, windsurfing and kitesurfing and paragliding in the Canary Islands before you book a lesson. The north of the island is also home to the Mirador del Río, which looks across to La Graciosa, and the calm white sand of Caletón Blanco near Órzola is the better choice for a swim.

beaches.name: Playa de Güigüí
beaches.tagline: Remote west-coast beach in a Gran Canaria nature reserve
beaches.summary: A remote beach on Gran Canaria's west coast inside the Güigüí special nature reserve. No road: you arrive on foot over the mountains or by sea. Plan a self-sufficient visit.
beaches.html:
Playa de Güigüí lies on the far west coast of Gran Canaria, in the municipality of La Aldea de San Nicolás, at the mouth of deep ravines that run down from the mountains to the sea. The land around it is the Güigüí special nature reserve (Reserva Natural Especial de Güigüí), protected for its cliffs, its old, deeply cut ravines and its plants, some of which grow nowhere else; several threatened seabird species nest on the coastal cliffs.

There is no road to the beach, and that is the whole point of coming. The way in on land is a long, steep mountain path over the ridge and down the ravine, a serious hike in full sun, and the same climb has to be done in reverse to get out. The other way in is by sea. Once there, you will find a wild beach backed by cliffs, where you should plan a self-sufficient visit. Do not rely on finding toilets, drinking water, shade or a lifeguard. This is open Atlantic coast: calm-looking water does not guarantee safe swimming.

Before you go

  • No road access: on foot by a long, steep path, or by sea.
  • Carry all your water, food and sun protection, and take your rubbish home.
  • Do not rely on services or a lifeguard, and do not assume calm-looking water is safe for swimming.
  • It is a protected reserve: stay on the path and leave plants and wildlife alone.

Güigüí suits experienced walkers: read our guide to hiking in the Canary Islands before you go. For an easier beach day on the same side of the island, the sheltered Playa de Amadores and the harbour at Puerto de Mogán are in the south-west, and Roque Nublo crowns the mountains inland.

beaches.name: Playa de La Concha and the El Cotillo lagoons
beaches.tagline: Calm, reef-sheltered white-sand coves at El Cotillo, north-west Fuerteventura
beaches.summary: Sheltered white-sand coves north of El Cotillo on Fuerteventura's north-west coast, with gentle waves. La Concha holds a Blue Flag in 2026.
beaches.html:
North of the fishing village of El Cotillo, on the north-west coast of Fuerteventura in the municipality of La Oliva, the shore breaks into a series of small coves known as the lagoons (Los Lagos). Low rocky reefs close each one off from the open sea, which keeps the water inside calm on most days. The best known is Playa de La Concha, a curve of white sand about 200 metres long and 50 metres wide that the La Oliva council describes as having gentle waves. La Concha is on the 2026 Blue Flag list published by ADEAC.

A little closer to the village, the beach the council lists as Los Lagos (Marfolín) is about 150 metres of white sand with gentle waves, and more small coves follow along the coast. The contrast with the coast just south of El Cotillo is sharp: Piedra Playa, the long golden beach on the other side of the village, is listed by the same council as having strong waves and is a surf beach. If the wind and swell are up, the lagoons are where families go.

Things to know

  • Blue Flag at La Concha in 2026. Check the flag and posted information before swimming.
  • The water is calm inside the reefs, but conditions outside them are much rougher; stay within the coves.
  • The reefs and rocks are sharp: water shoes help, especially at low tide.
  • The island tourism page confirms a lifeguard service at La Concha; check duty hours locally and keep children within reach.

El Cotillo is around the north coast from Corralejo, so it pairs well with a day on the Grandes Playas de Corralejo and the Corralejo dunes. Inland, the volcano walk at Calderón Hondo is a short drive away. See our best beaches in the Canary Islands guide for more calm-water options.

beaches.name: Playa de Las Canteras
beaches.tagline: Las Palmas de Gran Canaria's city beach behind the La Barra reef
beaches.summary: The city beach of Las Palmas de Gran Canaria: a long bay with a 3 km promenade, calm water behind the La Barra reef, surf at the southern end and lifeguards.
beaches.html:
Playa de Las Canteras curves along the western side of Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, the capital of Gran Canaria, near the port. It runs from the Alfredo Kraus Auditorium in the Guanarteme district to La Puntilla in La Isleta, with a pedestrian promenade about three kilometres long lined with cafés, ice-cream shops and fish restaurants. People swim, run, play football and surf here every day of the year.

What makes Las Canteras unusual for an Atlantic beach is La Barra, a long reef that runs parallel to more than half of the beach a short way offshore. The city's tourism board describes it as a limestone reef over 100,000 years old that acts as a natural breakwater, giving calm water in the central and northern sections; it can be exposed at low tide. The southern end, near the auditorium and the La Cícer area, has no such shelter and is where the surfers go. Muro Marrero and Playa Chica are the most family-friendly stretches, and La Puntilla is still home to local fishermen. On clear days you can see Tenerife and the peak of Teide across the water.

Good to know

  • Lifeguard and surveillance service, accessible toilets and assisted bathing.
  • Calmest water in the sections sheltered by La Barra; waves at La Cícer.
  • Sun loungers, sports areas and children's playgrounds at both ends.
  • A step-free route along the promenade for people with reduced mobility.

Las Canteras makes a good base for exploring the city: the old quarter of Vegueta, with the Casa de Colón, is a short bus ride away. Surfers should read our surfing guide, and during Carnival, the Las Palmas de Gran Canaria Carnival takes over the city. Gran Canaria Airport is on the east coast, south of the city.

beaches.name: Playa de las Conchas (La Graciosa)
beaches.tagline: La Graciosa's wild northern beach under Montaña Bermeja
beaches.summary: A long, wild beach on the north of La Graciosa, reached by ferry from Lanzarote then on foot or by bike. Stunning views, but strong currents and no lifeguards.
beaches.html:
Playa de las Conchas lies on the north coast of La Graciosa, the small island off the northern tip of Lanzarote that belongs to the municipality of Teguise. It is about 610 metres of fine pale sand under the red cone of Montaña Bermeja, looking straight out at the uninhabited islets of Montaña Clara and Alegranza and the Roque del Oeste and Roque del Este. The Teguise tourism office calls it probably the most spectacular beach on the island, and the colours are the reason: turquoise water, white foam, red mountain and black rock.

Getting there is part of the trip. Passenger ferries operated by Líneas Romero and Biosfera Express cross from the port of Órzola in the north of Lanzarote to Caleta de Sebo, La Graciosa's harbour village. The island has no asphalted roads, so from Caleta de Sebo you cross on sandy tracks, on foot or by bike; bikes can be hired in the village and need to be suited to off-road riding. There is nothing at the beach itself apart from litter bins, so carry water, food and sun protection for the whole day.

Bathing safety

  • The Teguise tourism office marks the beach with "No service of lifeguard and rescue".
  • Its second warning reads "Beach with waves and strong currents"; Spain's tourism site also lists windy conditions and strong waves.
  • Do not enter the water: the waves and strong currents make this a beach for enjoying from the sand.
  • Fires and barbecues are prohibited.

For calmer water on the same trip, the beaches on La Graciosa's south coast face Lanzarote and are more sheltered. Our island-hopping guide covers ferry options, and Caletón Blanco, just south of Órzola, is an easy swim stop on the way back.

beaches.name: Playa de las Teresitas
beaches.tagline: Santa Cruz de Tenerife's golden beach, built with Saharan sand
beaches.summary: A city beach in Tenerife: 1.3 km of golden sand under the Anaga hills near San Andrés, with calm water behind a breakwater and lifeguards.
beaches.html:
Playa de las Teresitas lies beside the fishing village of San Andrés, on the north-east coast of Tenerife, about 7 km from the centre of Santa Cruz de Tenerife. It is the city's beach: a straight run of golden sand some 1,300 metres long and 80 metres wide, lined with palm trees and backed by the steep, dry slopes at the edge of the Anaga hills. It is a popular beach with Santa Cruz residents.

The beach is man-made, and the sand is not from Tenerife. According to the Santa Cruz city council's official chronicler, the coast here once held three small black-sand beaches; to build the new one, five million sacks of sand were shipped in from the Sahara, and the beach opened on 15 June 1973. A breakwater about a kilometre long, built from large rocks, runs offshore to hold the sand in place and break the swell. That is why the water is so calm compared with the open north coast, and why the council describes it as ideal for children.

What to know before you go

  • The official Tenerife tourism site lists lifeguards. Check the service times posted at the beach.
  • Toilets, showers, sun loungers and parasols for hire, kiosks, bars and a stand-up paddle area.
  • A large car park sits behind the sand; city bus 910 runs from the Santa Cruz interchange.
  • Pets are not allowed on the beach.

Las Teresitas pairs easily with a day in Santa Cruz and its neighbour, the UNESCO-listed La Laguna old town, or with the Auditorio de Tenerife on the city seafront. The road beyond San Andrés climbs into Anaga Rural Park and down to the wild black sand of Playa de Benijo. The city celebrates the Santa Cruz de Tenerife Carnival.

beaches.name: Playa de Maspalomas
beaches.tagline: Gran Canaria's dune beach by the Maspalomas lighthouse
beaches.summary: A long golden beach in south Gran Canaria, backed by the protected Maspalomas dunes and the 1890 lighthouse. Blue Flag in 2026, with quiet naturist sections.
beaches.html:
Playa de Maspalomas runs along the southern tip of Gran Canaria, in the resort area of Maspalomas in the municipality of San Bartolomé de Tirajana. It begins at the Maspalomas lighthouse, a 56-metre tower first lit on 1 February 1890, and follows the shore east to the Punta de Maspalomas, where it turns the corner and becomes Playa del Inglés. It is the same continuous beach, and walking from one end to the other is something of a local habit.

Behind the sand lies the Maspalomas dune reserve, more than 400 hectares of wind-shaped sand together with La Charca, a brackish lagoon where migrating birds rest, and the Palmeral palm grove. The reserve is protected, and the island's tourism board asks visitors to always keep to the marked-out areas and authorised paths, to follow the signs, not to build stone structures and to respect plants and animals; camping is forbidden. Visitors can use the marked paths, but must not walk across or remain on the dunes themselves. On the beach, the long middle section is quieter and popular with naturists. The council locates the naturist area at La Punta or Cañada de la Penca. Surfing spots are found towards the wilder end of Playa del Inglés.

What to know

  • Blue Flag beach in 2026.
  • Stay on the marked paths through the dunes; camping is forbidden.
  • The council identifies a naturist area at La Punta or Cañada de la Penca.
  • Restaurants and shops along the promenade at the lighthouse end.

Read our guide to the Maspalomas dunes before you set out across the sand, and bring water and sun cover, as there is no shade once you leave the promenade. The beach continues east as Playa del Inglés, and the harbour at Puerto de Mogán is a short drive west along the coast.

beaches.name: Playa de Sotavento
beaches.tagline: Fuerteventura's long Jandía beach and windsurf arena
beaches.summary: A 6.5 km sweep of sand on the Jandía coast of south Fuerteventura, with a tidal lagoon and steady wind. Home of the windsurf world championship.
beaches.html:
Playa de Sotavento is the long beach on the south-east coast of the Jandía peninsula, in the municipality of Pájara in the south of Fuerteventura. The Pájara council lists it at 6,500 metres long and about 85 metres wide, running south-west from the Costa Calma area towards Risco del Paso. Sotavento means leeward: the name refers to its side of the peninsula, but this is still a windy beach.

That wind is what made Sotavento famous. The beaches here host the windsurf and wingfoil world championship; the Cabildo de Fuerteventura reported the start of its 36th edition in July 2024. Behind a long sand spit lies a shallow lagoon, marked on maps as the Laguna de Sotavento, which fills and empties with the tide. Away from the sailing, the beach is wide, open and very quiet, with sand that changes shape with every tide.

Things to know

  • Expect wind most days, especially in summer: good for sailing and walking, less so for a relaxed swim.
  • No lifeguard service is confirmed on an official page; swim with care and away from boards and kites.
  • The island tourism page lists parking, restaurants, showers, sunbeds, parasols and sports equipment. Services vary along the beach; bring water, sun protection and a windbreak.
  • The tide makes a big difference to the lagoon and the width of the beach; check tide times before you go.

Read our windsurfing and kitesurfing guide before booking a lesson. Further south, the road continues to Morro Jable and the track to wild Playa de Cofete; for gentler water in the north of the island, see the Grandes Playas de Corralejo. Most visitors arrive through Fuerteventura Airport.

beaches.name: Playa de Tazacorte
beaches.tagline: Dark-sand harbour beach on La Palma's sunny west coast, Blue Flag 2026
beaches.summary: The dark-sand beach at Puerto de Tazacorte on La Palma's west coast, with sunbeds, showers and a play area. Blue Flag in 2026 and west-facing for sunsets.
beaches.html:
Playa de Tazacorte is the beach of Puerto de Tazacorte, the harbour village of the municipality of Tazacorte on the west coast of La Palma. It lies at the mouth of the Barranco de las Angustias, the deep ravine that drains the Caldera de Taburiente National Park, and Spain's national tourism site notes that the ravine's mouth divides the beach in two. Like most beaches on La Palma it is volcanic: dark sand mixed with gravel, listed at 200 metres by Spain's national tourism site, with the village's houses and the harbour right behind it.

Unlike many of La Palma's wilder beaches, this one is well equipped. Spain's national tourism site lists sunshade and sun lounger rental, water-craft rental, showers, a sports area and a children's play area, and the village behind has places to eat. The beach, listed as El Puerto de Tazacorte, is on the 2026 Blue Flag list published by ADEAC. Swimming conditions are described as moderate waves, so check the flags and conditions before entering. Facing west, the beach is a classic place to watch the sun go down.

Practical points

  • Blue Flag beach in 2026. Check the flag and posted information before swimming.
  • Dark volcanic sand heats up quickly in the sun: bring footwear.
  • Sunbeds, umbrellas, showers and a children's play area are listed.
  • Reached by car, with parking in the village and by the harbour.

Tazacorte sits below the Aridane valley, a short drive from Los Llanos de Aridane and the trails into the Caldera. Combine a beach afternoon with a trip up to the observatories at the Roque de los Muchachos and an evening of stargazing. Flights to the island land at La Palma Airport, on the opposite coast.

facts.value: Parking in Puerto de Tazacorte village and by the harbour

beaches.name: Playa del Duque
beaches.tagline: Costa Adeje's polished resort beach, Blue Flag in 2026
beaches.summary: A 390-metre golden beach in the resort area of Costa Adeje, south Tenerife, with lifeguards, step-free access and a seafront promenade. Blue Flag in 2026.
beaches.html:
Playa del Duque sits at the northern end of Costa Adeje, on the sunny south-west coast of Tenerife. It is an upmarket stretch of the resort's shoreline: about 390 metres of golden sand, 60 metres wide, with large hotels, landscaped gardens and a promenade of restaurants and shops right behind it. The Adeje council's tourism site describes the beach as chosen by people looking for sun and quiet, and rates its occupancy as high.

The beach is well run. The 2026 Blue Flag list awarded by ADEAC names El Duque (Sur), the southern part of the beach. The council lists lifeguards, regular water testing, toilets, showers, sun loungers and parasols, and an accessible route with boardwalks over the sand, an accessible changing room and an amphibious bathing chair. The same page also flags strong currents. The water is open Atlantic, not a sheltered bay, so check the flag before you swim (red means no bathing, yellow means take care), swim parallel to the shore, and be careful with inflatables, which the council warns can carry you out to sea without you noticing.

Good to know

  • Blue Flag beach in 2026 (El Duque, southern section) with a lifeguard service.
  • Sun loungers and parasols for hire, showers, toilets, kiosks and bars.
  • Step-free access, an accessible toilet and changing room, and an amphibious chair.
  • The council warns of strong currents: follow the flags.

Playa del Duque is a short ride from Siam Park and from the boats that run whale and dolphin watching trips off the south-west coast. The sea cliffs of Los Gigantes are further north along the same coast, and the Teide cable car makes a good day away from the sand. Tenerife South Airport is the nearest airport.

beaches.name: Playa del Inglés
beaches.tagline: South Gran Canaria's big resort beach, joined to Maspalomas
beaches.summary: The wide, busy resort beach of Playa del Inglés in south Gran Canaria, joined to Maspalomas beach and the dunes. Blue Flag in 2026, popular with families.
beaches.html:
Playa del Inglés is the main beach of the resort of the same name, part of the Maspalomas tourist area on the south coast of Gran Canaria. It runs below the hotels and apartments of the resort and continues without a break round the Punta de Maspalomas to become Playa de Maspalomas. The official Canary Islands tourism site describes a family beach with services at the resort end and surfing spots and nudist zones towards the lighthouse.

The northern part, below the resort, is the busy end, with beach kiosks, groups of friends playing in the waves and runners on the hard sand. As you head south towards the dunes the hotels fall away. Towards the lighthouse the beach becomes wilder, with surfing spots and nudist zones, according to the official Canary Islands tourism site. The Maspalomas dunes rise straight behind this part of the beach; they are a protected reserve, and visitors are asked to keep to the marked-out areas and authorised paths.

Planning a day here

  • Blue Flag beach in 2026 (listed as El Inglés).
  • Wide sand and protected areas that suit families.
  • Busier near the resort; quieter towards the dunes.
  • Surfing spots and naturist zones towards the lighthouse.

Playa del Inglés is a natural starting point for a walk along the shore to the Maspalomas lighthouse, with the dunes on one side and the sea on the other. For a calmer swim in a sheltered bay, try Playa de Amadores further west, and for a day out of the resort, the drive up to Roque Nublo shows the island's mountain interior.

beaches.name: Playa Grande (Puerto del Carmen)
beaches.tagline: Puerto del Carmen's main town beach: calm water, Blue Flag, lifeguards
beaches.summary: The long golden beach in front of Puerto del Carmen on Lanzarote: calm water, lifeguards, sunbeds and a promenade of restaurants. Blue Flag in 2026.
beaches.html:
Playa Grande is the main beach of Puerto del Carmen, on Lanzarote, in the municipality of Tías on the island's south-east coast. It is also known as Playa Blanca, the name it carries on the Blue Flag list, so do not confuse it with the resort of Playa Blanca in the far south. It is a long, straight sweep of golden sand, about 1,190 metres according to the island tourism board, with the seafront promenade running its whole length.

The sea here is sheltered and the tourism board classes the water as calm, making it a family beach option in this part of Lanzarote. Follow the flags and lifeguard instructions. It is a fully serviced town beach: sunbeds and umbrellas to rent, showers, toilets, lifeguards, signage and restaurants along the promenade, with hotels and apartments just across the road. Playa Grande returned to the Blue Flag list in 2026, published by ADEAC, the Spanish body that runs the scheme. The shore faces south-east, so it gets the sun from early morning.

Practical points

  • Blue Flag beach in 2026, with a lifeguard service listed by Turismo Lanzarote.
  • Sunbeds, umbrellas, showers, toilets and restaurants on or beside the sand.
  • Reached by public bus; parking is listed among the services, though spaces near the promenade fill up in high season.
  • Follow the flags and lifeguard instructions, even when the water looks calm.

Puerto del Carmen is a good base for exploring the centre of the island: the wine country of La Geria and the César Manrique Foundation are within easy driving distance, and most visitors arrive through Lanzarote Airport. For a wilder beach day, drive south to the Playas de Papagayo.

facts.label: Parking
facts.value: Listed among the beach services; streets near the promenade fill up in high season

beaches.name: Playa Jardín
beaches.tagline: Puerto de la Cruz's black-sand beach in César Manrique gardens
beaches.summary: Black volcanic sand set in gardens by César Manrique in Puerto de la Cruz, north Tenerife. Breakwaters calm the swell; outside them the Atlantic can be rough.
beaches.html:
Playa Jardín ("garden beach") is the main beach of Puerto de la Cruz, on the north coast of Tenerife. The complex was designed by the Lanzarote artist César Manrique, who set the shore inside gardens of palms and tropical plants, with waterfalls, volcanic rock and paths running between them. It is really three beaches in a row: Playa Jardín itself (about 240 metres long), the smaller Playa Chica and Punta Brava at the western end, all of black volcanic sand.

This is the north coast, open to the Atlantic swell, and the sea here is a different animal from the sheltered south. Breakwaters have been built off the beach so you can swim more comfortably, and the official Tenerife tourism site warns that outside them the waves can get much stronger. Check the current bathing notices and water-quality information before entering, even inside the breakwaters. Watch the flags and keep children close when the swell is up. The beach has toilets, showers, bars and restaurants, sun loungers and parasols for hire, a children's area and a surf area, and all three sections have step-free access.

Before you go

  • Black volcanic sand that gets hot in strong sun: bring sandals.
  • Check bathing notices before swimming; the waves beyond the breakwaters can be fierce.
  • Toilets, showers, bars, a children's area and sun loungers for hire.
  • Step-free access and parking for more than 100 cars.

Playa Jardín is a short walk from the old centre of Puerto de la Cruz and very close to Loro Parque. The Orotava Valley rises behind the town towards Teide National Park, and in early summer nearby La Orotava lays its Corpus Christi flower and sand carpets. Tenerife North Airport is the closer of the island's two airports.

beaches.name: Playas de Papagayo
beaches.tagline: White-sand coves in the Los Ajaches natural monument, south Lanzarote
beaches.summary: A chain of sheltered white-sand coves east of Playa Blanca on Lanzarote, inside the Los Ajaches natural monument. Calm water, reached by dirt track.
beaches.html:
The Playas de Papagayo are a chain of small coves at the southern tip of Lanzarote, a short drive east of Playa Blanca in the municipality of Yaiza. They sit inside the Monumento Natural de Los Ajaches, a protected area of old, eroded volcanic hills, with no resort promenade behind the sand. There is a small beach bar on the hill above Papagayo. The Yaiza council lists seven beaches along this coast: Playa Mujeres, Playa de la Cruz (also called Playa del Pozo), Playa de la Cera, Playa del Papagayo, Caleta del Congrio, Puerto Muelas and the tiny Caletón de San Marcial.

The cove that gives the group its name is about 120 metres of fine white sand between two rocky headlands, and both the council and the island tourism board describe its water as calm. The rocks at either end are good for snorkelling. Playa Mujeres is the longest of the set at roughly 395 metres, while Caleta del Congrio, Puerto Muelas and Caletón de San Marcial are listed by the council as naturist beaches. On a clear day you can see Fuerteventura across the strait.

Getting there and the entry charge

  • Access is by unpaved track from the eastern edge of Playa Blanca, through a control point at the entrance to the natural monument.
  • As of November 2026 the Yaiza council lists a €3 entry charge for the Los Ajaches natural monument for motor vehicle access by non-residents of Lanzarote, payable by card only.
  • Parking is provided along the track; Turismo Lanzarote lists no public transport to the beaches.
  • The official regional tourism page lists no lifeguard surveillance. Parking and a hilltop beach bar are available; bring your own shade: bring water, food and sun protection.

Papagayo is the easy beach day from Playa Blanca, and it combines well with a drive up the west coast to El Golfo's green lagoon and the lava fields of Timanfaya National Park. For a town beach with sunbeds and lifeguards, try Playa Grande in Puerto del Carmen. Our guide to things to do in Lanzarote covers the rest of the island.
